Taiwan’s AI stock boom is creating more ways for investors to profit from its chip supply chain, making early-stage startups a tougher pitch. Taiwan’s benchmark Taiex index is up more than 50% this year, making it the world’s best-performing major index after pulling ahead of South Korea’s Kospi. The gains extend well beyond Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., spanning chip design, advanced packaging, networking, and server companies. About 7% of Taiwan-listed stocks have doubled this year, compared with 3% in South Korea.  That wider exposure has made Taiwan a preferred Asian AI trade. A September Bank of America survey found that 35% of fund managers expected Taiwan to benefit most from the next phase of the AI cycle, tying it with the US. Just 5% chose South Korea. For startups, the appeal of those public-market returns can reshape the funding calculation. For Anderson Chen, the founder and CEO of Operon Solutions, a Y Combinator-backed industrial AI startup, that calculus was part of what shaped how he raised money. Chen said he chose to raise Operon’s $700,000 pre-seed primarily from Silicon Valley investors, leaving room for Taiwanese friends and family to participate. “The market in semiconductors is just too good, and you can get 10X returns from the stock market,” Chen told Business Insider. In his view, even a successful startup IPO might generate only a two- or threefold return for investors. That creates a challenge for startups trying to build Taiwan’s next generation of winners. Caleb Chu, an early-stage investor and founder of Taiwan-based Nova Studio, which backs young founders, told Business Insider that the stock rally had drawn many Taiwanese investors toward listed shares and away from venture capital and startups. Findit, a government-commissioned platform that tracks Taiwan's startup ecosystem, found that seed and angel rounds made up 38.4% of investment deals by Taiwanese VC firms in 2021. By 2024, their share had fallen to 17.1%. By contrast, B- and C-round deals accounted for 39 deals, or 29.1% of the total, in 2024. Chu said Taiwanese investors had increasingly favored B- and C-round and pre-IPO companies, where the route to returns was clearer. Private-equity funds face a related, though not identical, pressure. A March report by KPMG Taiwan said TSMC’s share-price strength had created a “crowding-out effect” for private funds, as investors favored liquid public AI stocks over funds with longer lockups and less certain exits. US venture data shows a different, if still uneven, mix. PitchBook and the National Venture Capital Association said early-stage dealmaking was more favorable for AI startups than for non-AI peers in the first quarter of 2026. In a separate report, they found that 87.5% of US venture dollars invested in the first half went to rounds of $100 million or more. “When you look at the statistics around the world, the world is leaning toward early stage because investors realize it can generate much higher returns. Taiwan is the opposite,” Chu said. For founders, that can mean looking abroad for early backing. Operon's Chen said fundraising had become easier overall for Taiwanese deep-tech startups seeking overseas capital, helped by Taiwan’s technical talent and semiconductor expertise. His startup's $700,000 pre-seed round closed within three days. “It's gotten easier to fundraise in general, but maybe not necessarily in Taiwan,” he said. Jump to

Grand Theft Auto 6Grand Theft Auto VIGTA 6PS5XboxXbox Series X/S  Sony appears to have an exclusive marketing campaign with Rockstar Games for Grand Theft Auto 6. We don’t know what the terms of the deal were, but it has afforded the PlayStation maker all sorts of opportunities to announce things like “GTA 6 will play best on PS5.” The game is obviously also coming to Xbox, but Microsoft isn’t allowed to talk about that in its blog posts, so it stuffed an Xbox Series X inside of an alligator instead. “Measuring more than five feet from snout to tail, the console sits inside a meticulously crafted alligator, visible through an illuminated Xbox Nexus in its body,” the company announced today. “A custom Xbox Wireless Controller with bite marks rests between its jaws, complete with Xbox-green irises and Nexus-inspired pupils, making the Xbox Series X-BITE ready to play some of the biggest games of the year. The result is part-Xbox Series X, part-creature fabrication.” The ’80s-style synth-backed teaser for the limited edition Xbox makes the GTA-ness of it all clear despite never mentioning the game: The X-Bite isn’t being mass produced. The animatronic produced by John Nolan Studio, which has produced similar creatures for shows like The Witcher and movies like Jurassic World Dominion, is completely one-of-a-kind. The only way to obtain it is to win one of the special sweepstakes Xbox still loves doing. So why pull this stunt? Why put an illuminated Xbox power-on button inside the spiny scales of a five-foot gator? I suppose it was one Xbox marketing person’s clever workaround for the GTA 6 marketing exclusivity deal. “This November, Xbox is heading to Florida,” the blog post reads. Why is Xbox heading to Florida? The post never says. The words “Grand Theft Auto 6,” “Rockstar Games,” and “Vice City” are nowhere to be found. “Reminds me of companies that want to advertise around the Super Bowl but donât pay up so they have to say ‘The Big Game,'” wrote Giant Bomb cofounder Jeff Gerstmann on Bluesky. “‘Hey, if youâre going to sit down and play Big Florida Crime 6 this month, do it on a gator!'” GTA 6 will likely play the same on Xbox Series X as it does on PS5, as 99 percent of multiplatform games have this console generation. Larry Ellison has lost $159 billion, almost half his net worth, over the past year. The Bloomberg Billionaires Index shows Ellison's net worth has fallen by 49.2% to $164 billion, making him the world's ninth-richest person. He started the year ranked fifth — ahead of Mark Zuckerberg and behind Google's Sergey Brin. The 82-year-old's wealth is tied to his shares in Oracle, the tech company he cofounded in 1977. Its share price is down 39% since the start of 2026, and over 53% since November 2025. That included a nearly 9% drop on Monday as investors reacted to Oracle's announcement that it is issuing new shares and bonds to raise $20 billion. The stock fell another 1.5% in premarket trade on Tuesday. Investors are wary about the size of the raise, with growing concerns about how much Oracle is spending to build the data centers needed for its AI contracts, and whether it can deliver on the massive infrastructure expansion. The share sale would also dilute existing investors' stakes, and the added debt would heighten concerns about the company's already hefty borrowing. A broader tech sell-off has also reflected fears that the AI arms race is cooling. Google's parent company, Alphabet, had its worst post-earnings reaction last week, with its stock falling 13%. It's a sharp reversal from 2025, when Oracle stock surged on enthusiasm that it could become a major provider of AI infrastructure. In September 2025, Ellison was briefly the world's richest person as Oracle shares jumped some 40% in a single day. Apple shares fell as much as 4.43% in after-hours trading on Monday during the company’s fiscal Q4 2026 earnings call, before recovering some of those losses later in the evening. Here are the details. Apple today reported its fiscal Q4 2026 results, with a 12% increase in revenue, another 12% increase in net profit, and record revenue from its Services category, following its first sequential quarterly decline in 15 quarters. The results also included a 17% increase in iPhone revenue and a 24% increase in Mac revenue, but an 8% decline in Wearables, Home, and Accessories revenue, which Apple attributed to “a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year,” and a 10% decline in iPad revenue, which Apple attributed to supply constraints and a similarly difficult comparison against last year’s A16-powered iPad launch. During the conference call, Apple CEO John Ternus, CFO Kevan Parekh, and COO Sabih Khan fielded questions from analysts about rising memory costs, recent hardware price increases, and ongoing supply constraints, including those affecting the iPhone Duo. Hopefully Apple can use this aberration in trading algorithms to cancel as many shares as possible on the cheap!  The executives also offered a mixed outlook for the holiday quarter, with Apple expecting its highest quarterly revenue ever, but slower year-over-year growth, lower profit margins, and continued shortages of Mac and iPad models. After ending the regular trading session down 1.83%, Apple shares initially climbed 0.5% to $340.00 following the earnings release. However, as the conference call progressed, the stock reversed course, falling to $323.33, or 4.43% below Monday’s closing price. Shares then recovered some of those losses, ending the after-hours session at $328.81, down 2.81%. Of course, post-earnings after-hours trading doesn’t necessarily reflect how a stock will perform during the next day’s regular session, so it remains to be seen how investors will react when markets reopen on Tuesday after digesting tonight’s news. If you're considering Apple’s first foldable iPhone, know that getting your hands on it could take a while. During Monday's earnings call, Sabih Khan, Apple's chief operating officer, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo will catch up with demand. “So we're thrilled with the initial response on the iPhone Duo. iPhone Duo is constrained as of today,” Khan said in response to questions from a JPMorgan analyst. “The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible," Khan added. "But at this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance." The Duo was released on October 23, following preorders on October 16. The folding phone starts at $1,999 and opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Customers ordering online quickly faced a long wait, with delivery estimates slipping into late January 2027 shortly after preorders opened. The supply squeeze extends beyond Apple’s newest phone. Khan said that while strong demand constrained supplies of iPhones, Macs, and iPads during the September quarter, the biggest bottleneck was access to the advanced chipmaking technology used to produce Apple’s processors. “For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected,” Khan said. Apple is competing for memory with tech giants who are pouring money into AI data centers. Business Insider previously reported that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron supply chips for both consumer gadgets and AI infrastructure, and as manufacturers shift production toward the booming AI market, device makers face tighter supplies and higher costs. CFO Kevan Parekh said during the earnings call that, excluding tariff refunds, company and product gross margins would each have fallen about one percentage point sequentially, primarily because of higher memory costs. Windows 11 should feel a lot more responsive these days, especially on the new crop of laptops that focus on affordability and premium features.  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  Microsoft has been busy at work reducing the amount of RAM that Windows 11 consumes, and it finally made an official statement today on the topic. As it turns out, the company has already been quietly shipping performance improvements in the latest Windows 11 updates, focusing on making systems with 8GB of RAM feel a lot more responsive. The result? Microsoft says Windows 11 is now about 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs compared to before this work started. The work also applies to systems with 4GB, 16GB, and beyond, with specific tuning for each amount. This couldn't come at a better time. RAM and storage shortages (explained below) are driving up the cost of all PCs, and models with 8GB of RAM are being revived to lessen the burden on consumers.  Why you can trust Windows Central     Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.       Companies like Dell, Acer, and HP have all recently launched 8GB laptops that cost somewhere around $699, with student and regular discounts frequently dropping those numbers lower. If you were hesitant to shop for an 8GB laptop before, the recent Windows 11 updates should have you reconsidering, especially when prices are this reasonable. Here are my three favorite 8GB laptops right now. Dell's awesome XPS 13 starts at $699.99 (or $599.99 if you're a student) and includes an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 13.4-inch touch display with 2560x1600 resolution 👉 See at Dell.com Dell's new XPS 13 for 2026 wowed both Zac Bowden and me at Computex earlier this year, and it's been available to buy since June. It's a laptop with many premium features despite its price, including a higher-res 2560x1600 (QHD+) display with a 120Hz refresh rate, an IR camera for Windows Hello facial recognition, capable speakers, and a comfortable keyboard/touchpad combo. 👉 Does Acer's Swift Air 14 beat Dell's awesome XPS 13? It does not, however, offer USB-A or 3.5mm audio ports. Its display does not use an OLED panel; it uses IPS instead. And the $599 price is only available for students. Still, $699 for everyone else is not bad at all in this economy, and most users should have no issues with the XPS 13. HP's 14-inch OmniBook 5 is currently on sale for $599.99. It has an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 14-inch OLED touch display with 1920x1200 resolution. 👉 See at HP.com HP's OmniBook 5 14 comes with the same Intel Core 5 320 CPU as the other laptops in this roundup, so don't expect any major performance changes. The OmniBook 5 includes an OLED panel for deeper contrast and more vivid color than IPS. The tradeoff is a lower 1920x1200 resolution and lower 60Hz refresh rate compared to the XPS 13. HP's laptop also includes HDMI and 3.5mm audio ports alongside dual USB-C at 10Gbps. It's nice to have native video, but the lack of Thunderbolt is a letdown. This laptop is currently on sale for $599.99 for everyone, making it (temporarily) the best deal of the bunch. Acer's Swift Air 14 costs $699.99 and comes with an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 512GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 14-inch non-touch display at 1920x1200. 👉 See at BestBuy.com Acer's Swift Air 14 immediately makes an argument for itself with twice as much storage (512GB) as the Dell and HP laptops. For those who prefer to store locally, this could be the deciding factor. However, it does drop down to PCIe 3.0 speeds. Performance is largely the same thanks to it having the Intel Core 5 320 chip inside, with 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM. The display hits a 1920x1200 resolution; it doesn't have touch, but it does hit a smoother 120Hz refresh rate. You're definitely giving up some screen quality to land that extra storage. While the keyboard is great, the touchpad leaves something to be desired. Your experience may vary.      Sure, Windows 11 could always be more streamlined, but this big push for more RAM efficiency is also a result of the ongoing memory and storage crisis. See, AI data centers are eating up many of the foundational components of PCs, making the consumer side far more expensive. RAM in particular has exploded in price; the same 32GB kit of DDR5 I bought for my gaming PC a few years ago, for example, is roughly 600% more expensive today. Storage isn't much better. This is forcing PC makers to reevaluate their product lineups, as many consumers can no longer afford PCs with 16GB or more of RAM. Cutting RAM in half is a huge cost saver and won't likely stop anytime soon (the RAM crisis could last for years to come), so it's great to see Microsoft taking user complaints about Windows 11's responsiveness (or lack thereof) seriously. [Editor’s note: Steve Jobs  had a lot to say Monday during his  conference call with analysts following Apple’s announcement of  record earnings and sales. Here’s the Apple CEO in his own words.] Hi, everybody. As most of you know, I don’t usually participate in Apple earnings calls, since you’re all in such capable hands with Peter and Tim. But I just couldn’t help dropping by for our first 20-billion-dollar quarter. I’d like to chat about a few things, and then stay for the rest of the Q&A, if that’s all right. First, let me discuss iPhone. We sold 14.1 million iPhones in the quarter, which represents a 91 percent unit growth over the year-ago quarter, and was well ahead of IDC’s latest published estimate of 64 percent growth for the global smartphone market in the September quarter. And it handily beats RIM’s 12.1 million BlackBerrys sold, in their most recent quarter ending in August. We’ve now passed RIM. And I don’t see them catching up with us in the foreseeable future. They must move beyond their area of strength and comfort, into the unfamiliar territory of trying to become a software platform company. I think it’s going to be a challenge for them to create a competitive platform and to convince developers to create apps for yet a third software platform after iOS and Android. With 300,000 apps on Apple’s App Store, RIM has a high mountain ahead of them to climb.     But what about Google? Last week, Eric Schmidt reiterated that they are activating 200,000 Android devices per day, and have around 90,000 apps in their app store. For comparison, Apple has activated around 275,000 iOS devices per day on average for the past 30 days, with a peak of almost 300,000 iOS devices per day on a few of those days. And Apple has 300,000 apps on its App Store. Unfortunately, there is no solid data on how many Android phones are shipped each quarter. We hope that manufacturers will soon start reporting the number of Android handsets they ship each quarter, but today that just isn’t the case. Gartner reported that about 10 million Android phones were shipped in the June quarter, and we await to see if iPhone or Android was the winner in this most recent quarter. Google loves to characterize Android as “open,” and iOS and iPhone as “closed”. We find this a bit disingenuous, and clouding the real difference between our two approaches. The first thing  most of us think about when we hear the word “open” is Windows, which is available on a variety of devices. Unlike Windows, however, where most PCs have the same user interface and run the same apps, Android is very fragmented. Many Android OEMs, including the two largest, HTC and Motorola, install proprietary user interfaces to differentiate themselves from the commodity Android experience. The user’s left to figure it all out. Compare this with iPhone, where every handset works the same. Twitter client [TweetDeck] recently launched their app for Android. They reported that they had to contend with more than a hundred different versions of Android software on 244 different handsets. The multiple hardware and software iterations present developers with a daunting challenge. Many Android apps work only on selected Android handsets, running selected Android versions. And this is for handsets that have been shipped less than 12 months ago! Compare this with iPhone, where there are two versions of the software, the current and the most recent predecessor, to test against. In addition to Google’s own app marketplace, Amazon, Verizon, and Vodafone have all announced that they are creating their own app stores for Android. So there will be at least four app stores on Android, which customers must search among to find the app they want, and developers will need to work with to distribute their apps and get paid. This is gonna be a mess for both users and developers. Contrast this with Apple’s integrated App Store, which offers users the easiest-to-use largest app store in the world, preloaded on every iPhone. Apple’s app store has over three times as many apps as Google’s marketplace, and offers developers one-stop shopping to get their apps to market easily, and get paid swiftly. You know, even if Google were right, and the real issue is “closed” versus “open,” it is worthwhile to remember that open systems don’t always win. Take Microsoft’s “Plays For Sure” music strategy, which used the PC model—which Android uses as well—of separating the software components from the hardware components. Even Microsoft finally abandoned this “open” strategy in favor of copying Apple’s integrated approach with their Zune player, unfortunately leaving their OEMs empty-handed in the process. Google flirted with this integrated approach with their Nexus One phone. In reality, we think the open versus closed argument is just a smokescreen to try and hide the real issue, which is, “What’s best for the customer – fragmented versus integrated?” We think Android is very, very fragmented, and becoming more fragmented by the day. And as you know, Apple strives for the integrated model so that the user isn’t forced to be the systems integrator. We see tremendous value at having Apple, rather than our users, be the systems integrator. We think this a huge strength of our approach compared to Google’s: when selling the users who want their devices to just work, we believe that integrated will trump fragmented every time. And we also think that our developers could be more innovative if they can target a singular platform, rather than a hundred variants. They can put their time into innovative new features, rather than testing on hundreds of different handsets. So we are very committed to the integrated approach, no matter how many times Google tries to characterize it as “closed.” And we are confident that it will triumph over Google’s fragmented approach, no matter how many times Google tries to characterize it as “open.” Second, I’d like to comment on the “avalanche” of tablets poised to enter the market in the coming months. First, it appears to be just a handful of credible entrants, not exactly an avalanche. Second, almost all of them use seven-inch screens, as compared to iPad’s near 10-inch screens. Let’s start there. One naturally thinks that a seven-inch screen would offer 70 percent of the benefits of a 10-inch screen. Unfortunately, this is far from the truth. The screen measurements are diagonal, so that a seven-inch screen is only 45 percent as large as iPad’s 10-inch screen. You heard me right: just 45 percent as large. If you take an iPad and hold it upright in portrait view, and draw an imaginary horizontal line halfway down the screen, the screens on these seven-inch tablets are a bit smaller than the bottom half of the iPad’s display. This size isn’t sufficient to create great tablet apps, in our opinion. While one could increase the resolution of the display to make up some of the difference, it is meaningless unless your tablet also includes sandpaper, so that the user can sand down their fingers to around one-quarter of their present size. Apple has done extensive user testing on user interfaces over many years, and we really understand this stuff. There are clear limits of how close you can physically place elements on a touchscreen before users cannot reliably tap, flick or pinch them. This is one of the key reasons we think the 10-inch screen size is the minimum size required to create great tablet apps. Third, every tablet user is also a smartphone user. No tablet can compete with the mobility of a smartphone. Its ease of fitting into your pocket or purse. Its unobtrusiveness when used in a crowd. Given that all tablet users will already have a smartphone in their pockets, giving up precious display area to fit a tablet in their pockets is clearly the wrong trade-off. The seven-inch tablets are tweeners: too big to compete with a smartphone, and too small to compete with an iPad. Fourth, almost all of these new tablets use Android software, but even Google is telling the tablet manufacturers not to use their current release—Froyo—for tablets, and to wait for a special tablet release next year. What does it mean when your software supplier says not to use their software in your tablet, and what does this mean when you ignore them and use it anyway? Fifth, iPad now has over 35,000 apps on the App Store. This new crop of tablets will have near zero. And sixth and last, our potential competitors are having a tough time coming close to iPad’s pricing, even with their far smaller, far less expensive screens. The iPad incorporates everything we’ve learned about building high-value products, from iPhones, iPods and Macs. We create our own A4 chip, our own software, our own battery chemistry, our own enclosure, our own everything. And this results in an incredible product at a great price. The proof of this will be in the pricing of our competitors’ products, which will likely offer less, for more. These are among the reasons that we think that the current crop of seven-inch tablets are going to be DOA—Dead on Arrival. Their manufacturers will learn the painful lesson that their tablets are too small, and increase the size next year, thereby abandoning both customers and developers who jumped on the seven-inch bandwagon with an orphaned product. Sounds like lots of fun ahead.   The iPad is clearly gonna affect notebook computers. And I think the iPad proves it’s not a question of if, it’s a question of when. And there’s I think a lot of development and progress over the next few years. But we’re already seeing tremendous interest in iPad from education and, much to my surprise, from business. We haven’t pushed it real hard in business, and it’s being grabbed out of our hands. And I talk to people every day in business, in all kinds of businesses, that are using iPads. All the way from boards of directors that are shipping iPads around instead of board books, down to nurses and doctors and hospitals, and other large and small businesses.  So the more time that passes, the more I am convinced that we’ve got a tiger by the tail here,and this is a new model of computing which, you know, we’ve already got tens of millions of people already trained on with the iPhone. And that lends itself to lots of different aspects of life, both personal, educational, and business. So I see it as very general purpose, and I see it as really big. And the timing, one could argue about the timing endlessly, but I don’t think one could argue that it’s gonna happen anymore.  [Q: You think this could be your second biggest business behind iPhone?]  I try to not predict, I try to just report, so we’ll keep you posted. As you know, we’re already shipping more of them than Macs after just a few quarters.  [Q: Any updates on your stance on Flash?]  Flash memory? We love flash memory.  [Q: You are the tablet market right now… This is the second time you’ve come on to talk about competition, and I’m just wondering if much like Apple encroaching on RIM’s monopoly in enterprise, if you think Apple is gonna be able to sustain share growth for tablets amid some of those new competitive headwinds. Some of those players may try different things and strategies, like tethering and Flash, multitasking, less content and app restrictions, and subsidized pricing. Just wondered if you think that may create itself a more fragmented market.]  I have a hard time envisioning what those strategies you mentioned are. In terms of pricing, so far the little we’ve seen, the tablets with far less functionality are having a hard time matching us in price. Flash hasn’t presented any problem at all—as you know, most of the video on web is now available in HTML5. And having the iTunes media store and over 35,000 apps on the App Store for iPad dwarfs anything else. And we think we have a very good product here that’s gonna be hard to match, and we’re not done, we’re working on a lot of things for the future. So I don’t know what exactly these strategies are, and we’ve priced iPad pretty aggressively. So we’re out to win this one.  [Q: Is the phone market a zero-sum game?]  As you know, the largest market of phones today around the world are non-smartphones. And so over the next several years, many of those non-smartphones are going to convert to smartphones. And the pie is gonna continue to grow. And I think there’ll be room for some number of companies to be successful, but eventually as most of those phones do convert to smartphones, it will turn into a zero-sum game, or at least a lot closer to that. I think right now it’s a battle for the mindshare of developers and for the mindshare of customers, and right now iPhone and Android are winning that battle.  [Q: What are your thoughts about Apple TV and how it’s going, since it seems to be on a streaming model now.]  We have gone to a streaming model on Apple TV. It’s complete streaming. So all the content is rented from the iTunes store, or is streamed from your computer, or soon to be streamed from your iPhone or iPad with AirPlay. And so how our new model of Apple TV doing? Well, I can report that in just a very short amount of time we’ve already sold a quarter million of them. Over 250,000. And we’re thrilled with that. I think that it’s a great product, and I think that its $99 price point is very enticing, and I think that when we get the AirPlay stuff in place before the end of this year, it’s gonna give another big reason for people to buy it. So we’re happy with how it’s turned out.  [Q: Biggest risks?]  Our goal is to make the best devices in the world, not to be the biggest. As you know, Nokia’s the biggest. And we admire them for being able to ship the number of handsets that they do. But we don’t aspire to be like them. They’re good at being like them. We want to be like us. And we want to make the best ones. So, you know, in our part of the market Android is our biggest competitor. They outshipped us in the June quarter as we were transitioning to iPhone 4, they outshipped us for the first time according to Gartner’s numbers, which we think are pretty accurate. And so we’re waiting to find out what happened in this quarter. And we’ll find out—I don’t know how we’ll find out, but Gartner will put out some new numbers, and maybe others will, and so one of these days we’ll eventually learn. And I imagine we’ll be competing with them for quite some time, but we have very different approaches. And we believe in our approach very strongly: providing users products that just work. And we think there’s lots of users that want that, in the world. And their approach is very different from that. And there may be lots of users that want their approach as well, but we’re going to pursue ours, and we think that’s the winning approach in the end.  [Q: Market share question.]  Nokia makes $50 handsets, and we don’t know how to make a great smartphone for $50. We’re not smart enough to have figured that one out yet, but believe me I’ll let you know when we do. And so our goal is to make really breakthrough great products, make the best products in every industry that we compete in, and to drive the cost down while constantly making the products better at the same time. That’s what we did with iPod. We updated our products many times every year with better functionality, often times at same price and sometimes at a lower price. And it was the relentless improvement at in some cases a lower price, that was able to beat our competition and yield the market share that it did. And as you know we have a very low market share in the phone market, in the single digits, in terms of all the handsets. And we have a very high market share now in tablets, because we’re the first mover. But we don’t think about it that way. The reason we wouldn’t make a seven-inch tablet isn’t because we don’t want to hit a price point, it’s because we don’t think you can make a great tablet with a seven-inch screen. We think it’s too small to express the software that people want to put on these things. And we think, as a software-driven company, we think about the software strategies first. And we know that software developers aren’t going to deal real well with all these different sized products, when they have to re-do their software every time a screen size changes, and they’re not going to deal well with products where they can’t put enough elements on the screen to build the kind of apps they want to build. So when we make decisions on seven-inch tablets, it’s not about cost, it’s about the value of the product when you factor in the software. You see what I’m getting at? So we’re all about making the best products at aggressive prices. And that’s what we will do. And that’s what we’ve done with the iPod, and that’s what we will do with the iPad as well. You’re looking at it wrong. You’re looking at it as a hardware person in a fragmented world. You’re looking at it as a hardware manufacturer that doesn’t really know much about software, who doesn’t think about an integrated product but assumes the software will somehow take care of itself. And you’re sitting around saying, well, how can we make this cheaper? Well, we can put a smaller screen on it, and a slower processor, and less memory, and you assume that the software will somehow just come alive on this product that you’re dreaming up, but it won’t. Because these app developers have taken advantage of the products that came before, with faster processors, with larger screens, with more capabilities that they can take advantage of to make better apps for customers. And they’re not… it’s a hard one, because it throws you right back into the beginning of that chicken-and-egg problem again, to change all the assumptions on these developers. Most of them will not follow you. Most of them will say, “I’m sorry, but I’m not going to write down a watered-down version of my app just because you’ve got this phone that you can sell for $50 less, and you’re begging me to write software for it.”  [Q: Why not return some of your cash to shareholders?]  We strongly believe that one or more very strategic opportunities may come along, that we are in a unique position to take advantage of because of our strong cash position. You know, we’ve demonstrated a strong track record of being very disciplined with the use of our cash. We don’t let it burn a hole in our pocket, we don’t allow it to motivate us to do stupid acquisitions. And so I think that we’d like to continue to keep our powder dry, because we do feel that there are one or more strategic opportunities in the future. That’s the biggest reason.  [Q: Why do you think you have an advantage on the price point for iPad versus PC manufacturers?]  I think part of it is because we engineer so much of it ourselves. The A4 chip inside it is an Apple creation. Everything from the battery chemistry to the enclosures. And we’ve learned a lot from the miniaturization we’ve done on iPods and iPhones, and we’re a very high-volume consumer electronics manufacturer. So I think we’ve learned a lot, we’ve developed a lot of our own components where others have to buy them on the market with middlemen, you know, getting their cut of things. And I think we’re systems architects and known how to build systems in a very efficient way. So I think this is a product we’ve been training for for the last decade.

Fortunately, the holidays only amplify our never-ending quest to find the latest and greatest deals, and we've found a nice collection of tablets that have something to offer beyond decent savings. For those looking for something to stream movies on while they're in bed, Amazon has an entrant from its own Fire tablet lineup that can be had for less than $100. Elsewhere, one retailer is offering some considerable savings on one of Microsoft's higher-end tablet options. Lastly, Amazon Prime members can also save big on a TCL tablet that has its own unique set of features — but even at its regular price, it's a device that can be a compelling option for those wanting an impressive display. If you've been noticing the signs that it may be time to upgrade your old tablet, the products below have been well-reviewed by either critics or actual customers, and we also kept various budgets in mind when determining this list. Of course, there can be plenty of Android tablets actually worth your money in 2026, so by no means is this list comprehensive. However, if you're shopping for yourself or looking for a gift for someone else, the devices below may just help get your holiday shopping done a bit earlier than you may have expected. Starting off our list is a tablet that's available for less than $100 while still having a familiar name attached to it. Available for 53% off its listed retail price, the Amazon Fire HD 10 tablet is available directly through the retailer for significantly less than its typical $154.99 MSRP. The specs certainly reflect the price, but prospective buyers should be aware that this model also includes lock screen ads. Users should also know an Amazon Fire tablet has plenty of cool tricks up its sleeve. The Amazon Fire HD 10 includes a 10.1-inch 1080p Full HD display with a 1,920-by-1,200 resolution — that's over 2 million pixels. Alongside up to 4 GB of RAM and 32 GB of storage (expandable up to 1 TB with microSD), the Fire 10 also includes a 5 MP front-facing camera and a 5 MP rear camera, both of which support 1080p video recording. Amazon promises up to 13 hours of battery life as well as a four-hour charge time through USB-C 2.0. Holding a 4.5-star rating with over 45,180 reviews, customers appreciate this Amazon's Choice item for its overall value, with many stating it can make a solid device for streaming entertainment. Finding it suitable for kids, customers also give it high marks for its clear display and ease of use. Looking at the negatives, however, users do seem mixed about the battery life, whereas some users find the tablet overall to be slow. Nonetheless, this one may be worth a closer look just for the sub-$100 price. Depending on your storage needs, retailer Best Buy currently has a solid deal on the Microsoft Surface Pro 13-inch OLED touchscreen tablet that can save buyers a good chunk of money. Users can either shave $300 off the typical $1,799.99 listing price for the 512 GB model, or they can upgrade to the 1 TB model for $450 off the usual $2,099.99 price. Either way, customers can access a high-end Microsoft tablet for less than the usual price, and either one will still gain you entry into the world of Microsoft Copilot+. With a 13-inch OLED screen supporting a 2,800-by-1,920 resolution and HDR, this tablet also includes a 12-core Snapdragon X2 Elite processor with an NPU that can perform 80 trillion operations per second (TOPS). With a 2-in-1 design that includes touchscreen support, the machine also supports Windows Ink styluses — a great reason those editing photos on a monitor may want to consider the Surface Pro. Along with 16 GB of DDR5 RAM, this tablet also includes two USB-C ports while offering DisplayPort support. Microsoft also promises 15.5 hours of battery life and fast charging. At Best Buy, this tablet holds a 4.5-star rating, though only 42 customers have reviewed it. In a review for Gadget Salvation, however, one critic noted that the CPU gain from this tablet is rather small when compared against the prior Snapdragon X Elite — though they did note a significant graphical improvement. Ultimately, the reviewer compliments the battery life while also mentioning this tablet could even be a computer replacement. Between the high-end Microsoft option and the lower-end Amazon offering, we wanted to include one last tablet that sits in the middle of these two extreme price points, and the TCL Nxtpaper 11 Plus fits the bill nicely. Only Amazon Prime members are going to be able to save 24% off the typical $369.99 listing price, but those with an eye for art may still find this device appealing. The big draw behind this tablet is that it includes an 11.5-inch Nxtpaper 4.0 display that offers a paper-like experience. Along with a 120 Hz 2.2K display that TCL promises is good for drawing, taking notes, and even alleviating eye strain, the Nxtpaper 11 Plus also includes a 3-in-1 VersaView Mode that allows users to switch between three different display modes. Additionally, users will get the T-Pen Stylus with this tablet, which features 4,096 pressure levels for precision. For battery life, this machine includes an 8,000 mAh battery alongside 33 W fast charging. All of this is packaged with 256 GB of storage, Android 15, and a MediaTek Helio G100 processor, which likely helps the tablet maintain a 4.4-star rating with over 340 reviews on Amazon. Users appreciate how easy the display is on their eyes, and several also compliment the device's battery life. However, at least one customer notes the device can be slow to boot. As for our own opinion, at least one member of our team considered buying a model from the Nxtpaper 11 lineup just for its screen. One of the largest determining factors for this list was price, as we wanted to find tablets that offered the best discounts prior to Black Friday. Along with choosing from a variety of devices that may suit a customer's budget, we also looked at customer and professional reviews for each of the tablets on this list. We made sure that each device holds a 4-star rating based on hundreds of reviews, when applicable. Just because a device has a deal doesn't mean it's worth buying, so we also favored familiar name brands when curating this selection. Bonus points were also given to Amazon's Choice items.

The Mbappe controversy demonstrates how market power in sport is being used to enforce conformity. Senior Editor for Inclusive Storytelling at The New Humanitarian. Save Share French football superstar Kylian Mbappe recently landed in trouble over a meme. Discussing an image that apparently superimposed his face on Mao Zedong’s, he referred to the late Chinese leader as someone he thought was a dictator, without naming Mao. The offhand remark became an international controversy. Chinese sponsors withdrew their support. State television suspended La Liga broadcasts. Apologies followed from Mbappe and his club, Real Madrid, while the league expressed regret over the offence caused.     Mbappe was riffing on one of the running jokes about his outsized influence over his clubs and teammates. He was not delivering a considered assessment of Chinese history. Yet the response turned a passing remark into a test of respect for an entire nation. Mbappe is not the first athlete to discover how quickly political sensitivities become instruments of discipline. A decade ago, American football star Colin Kaepernick knelt during the United States national anthem to protest systemic racism and police killings of Black people, and was effectively frozen out of the National Football League. In May, after Spanish footballer Lamine Yamal waved a Palestinian flag during Barcelona’s title celebrations, Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, accused him of inciting hatred and demanded that the club distance itself from the gesture. Kaepernick and Yamal made deliberate statements. Mbappe made a joke. Yet the distinction offered the latter little protection. An athlete need not deliberately enter politics to discover how tightly his speech is policed. Mbappe’s extraordinary visibility gives him influence and makes him commercially valuable. But the commercial relationships that make him valuable also hand others the means to discipline him. The logic is an old one. In ancient Greece, victorious athletes could receive substantial rewards from their cities, including money, meals at public expense and civic honours. Sporting success could open a path to political influence, and their achievements brought prestige to the communities that claimed them. But the claim could become possessive. According to the ancient Greek geographer and writer Pausanias, the runner Astylus, originally associated with Croton, later proclaimed himself a Syracusan when competing at the Olympic Games. His former compatriots responded by pulling down his statue and converting his house into a prison. Today, sporting institutions make similar claims on the people whose achievements they celebrate. The athlete represents the nation, embodies the club, carries the sponsor’s values. Each relationship becomes a reason to keep an inconvenient thought to oneself. As Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho put it, “Often the best thing you can do is keep your mouth shut, because there’s danger in so many things you say or comment on.” When a single remark threatens access to a market, the club and the league acquire a financial interest in treating it as misconduct, and the pressure to recant can be extreme. When a state broadcaster suspends an entire league, it punishes thousands of players, staff and viewers who had nothing to do with the remark, effectively holding them hostage to one man’s apology. That is market power being used to enforce conformity. This is where the contradictions of celebrity become especially apparent. Sporting businesses sell courage, authenticity and individual character. They encourage audiences to identify with the person behind the performance. But the expression of that character becomes a problem when it threatens another part of the business. The athlete is invited to be themselves, subject to approval. Further, audiences add their own pressure. We increasingly expect sports stars to address moral and political questions, and we judge their silence as well as their speech. Fame does carry obligations. But athletic excellence does not confer political wisdom, and prominence is not a qualification. If we want courage from athletes, we must also confront the institutions that make courage professionally dangerous. Mbappe’s case is revealing precisely because he was not taking a heroic stand. The freedom to speak cannot depend on an athlete being historically knowledgeable, perfectly articulate or deliberately brave. It must leave room for an uncertain remark and a foolish joke, as well as a carefully planned protest. However, it is clear that freedom does not confer immunity from critique. Fans can disagree loudly, and athletes should answer for objectionable speech. But the test should be whether a remark harms people, not whether it embarrasses a state or threatens a balance sheet. The supposed neutrality of sport helps to hide these demands for conformity. Flags, anthems and governments’ pursuit of prestige already fill sporting spectacles with political meaning. Athletes’ independent expression, on the other hand, attracts demands for silence when it disrupts those authorised messages. Yet though bringing honour to a community, a champion’s achievement does not give that community ownership over them. Clubs can purchase sporting services. Sponsors can purchase advertising. Neither transaction entitles anyone to dictate an athlete’s convictions. If sporting institutions insist on selling us the person behind the performance, they must accept that the person has a voice of their own. For more than 25 years, I have heard the same complaints from local marketing teams. “This doesn’t sound like us.” “Our customers don’t ask that question.” “That product isn’t even sold here.” “Why are we publishing a U.S. case study on the Japanese site?” At headquarters, these complaints were usually treated as resistance. Local teams simply wanted control, and they didn’t understand the cost of supporting 30 or 40 markets. They were slowing down a process that had been carefully engineered for speed and consistency. I understood that view. I also spent a lot of time explaining the local side of the argument to global teams who weren’t necessarily happy to hear it. Now AI is giving enterprises the ability to produce content for every market faster and more cheaply than ever. And AI search is showing us, very clearly, what happens when that content is the same everywhere. The local teams may have been right all along. This article examines why the traditional global content model is breaking down in AI search, and how to build an AI-powered content factory that scales without erasing what makes each market unique. Most multinational content operations were designed to solve one problem: how to publish the same message in many languages without the cost growing at the same rate as the number of markets. The industry developed very good tools for that problem: The key performance indicators followed the same logic: cost per word, TM leverage, reducing turnaround time, and accelerating time-to-market for a global launch. A high TM match rate was the key to maximizing KPIs and building confidence in uniform messaging. When local teams pushed back, the rationale for pushback was hard to quantify. It was typically framed in terms of tone, nuance, or lack of cultural fit. When matched against a dashboard of cost savings, “it doesn’t feel local” rarely won the argument. In traditional search, the cost of that decision was manageable. Hreflang told search engines which language and country version to show, so a translated page could still rank in its market. If the page was thin, it usually ranked a little lower. It didn’t disappear. See also: Lost In Translation: How Language Changes Which Brand AI Recommends AI search changes the unit of competition. Traditional search selected a page. AI search builds an answer from facts, passages, and evidence collected from many sources. That shift exposes a significant problem the traditional efficiency model created. When search engines find a cluster of pages that are essentially the same, they don’t fully process and store every version. One version is selected as the canonical and processed in full. The others are treated more like alternate names that point back to it, carrying only enough information (URL, language, country) to be served in the right context. AI systems refer to this as canonical tokenization, the process by which text across different languages is split, compressed, and processed. It is efficient for the search engine, and it works reasonably well when the job is to swap one URL for another on a results page. It works much less well when an AI system is retrieving passages to build an answer. The passage it retrieves often comes from the canonical version, and once that passage is pulled out of the page, it no longer carries the URL that told everyone which market it belonged to. I described the result in How AI’s Geo-Identification Failures Are Rewriting International SEO: When markets look the same, the strongest instance of your content wins. In most global companies, that is the U.S. or main English site. So a buyer in Germany may get U.S. product availability. A patient in Japan may read about a product or use that is not approved there. A Spanish-language query from Spain may be answered with content written for Mexico. This is the uncomfortable part for those of us who built global content programs. Translation memory was designed to maximize content reuse at scale. AI retrieval systems are designed to discard reuse. Every sentence we reused across 30 markets now makes those markets look more alike to a machine. The higher our TM leverage, the stronger the case that our local pages were alternate versions of one global page, not unique sources worth retrieving in their own right. When local teams said “this doesn’t feel like our market,” they were describing exactly what an AI system now concludes. The twin engines of the marketing agility framework describe two forces every multinational has to run at the same time: Research on the framework found that organizations perform best when both engines are running. Most global content programs, however, were built almost entirely around the global engine. The local engine was treated as a cost to be minimized, because local responsiveness was expensive. Every market-specific page needed a writer, a reviewer, and a budget line. That is the part AI changes. The usual way enterprises use AI today is to make the global engine faster: translate more content into more languages with fewer people. That produces more of the same near-identical pages, only quicker. It is a faster photocopier. The bigger opportunity is to use AI to make the local engine more affordable. If AI handles the tedious and time-consuming activities of drafting, translation, structuring, and formatting, people in each market can spend their time on what only they can provide: local evidence, local questions, and local judgment. A content factory built for AI search starts from a different premise. The product isn’t pages. The product is governed, market-scoped knowledge, and pages are one of the ways that knowledge is published. Before anything is written or translated, the organization needs a single source of truth where its important claims live. Each fact should record: This sounds like a governance exercise, and it is. It is also the only reliable way to prevent a fact that is true in one market from being published or retrieved as if it were true in all of them. This is the most important change to the translation workflow. Not every sentence should be treated the same way. Translation memory is still valuable for the first category. Product names, for example, should be identical across languages so that AI systems recognize them as the same entity. It is, however, a mistake to let TM leverage fill the second category. When a market-variable slot is empty, the factory should flag it, not copy the U.S. version into it. With the fact registry and the segment rules in place, AI can now handle most of the production work by drafting from approved facts, translating and structuring pages around real questions, and verifying that the right source has been integrated for every market-variable slot. This is where the cost savings come from now. The savings don’t come from reusing more sentences. They come from automating everything related to local evidence, so local teams can supply that evidence without bearing the full cost of producing the page. The global engine contributes what should be identical everywhere; the local engine contributes what must differ. Both meet in the fact registry, and AI assembles each market’s pages from it. “Keeping the human touch” is often understood as keeping a human post-editor at the end of the machine translation process. That role is becoming harder to defend on quality alone. A recent localization benchmark published here on Search Engine Journal found AI workflows outscored human translators in four of six content types. I don’t read that as the end of human involvement. I read it as a signal that the human value has moved upstream. In an AI content factory, people in each market are needed at four points: Notice that these are the same things local teams were complaining about for years. They were never really asking for better translation. They were asking for their market’s reality to be represented. This also changes how global SEO and content teams should be organized. The roles and service-level agreements I described in Effective SEO Organizational Structure For A Global Company need to include ownership of local evidence, not only local publishing. Because AI systems retrieve passages that lose their URL context, each important passage has to carry its own market information. A few simple rules make a large difference: These rules are easy to build into an AI-assisted workflow. They are much harder to apply consistently when 40 vendors are translating by hand. Most global teams can tell you how many pages they published per market. Very few can tell you what an AI assistant says about them in each market. That measurement should be part of the factory, not a one-time audit. Build a fixed set of priority prompts for each market, in the local language, and run them across the major AI assistants on a regular schedule. Then track four things: Market leakage is the metric I’d watch most closely. It is the most direct measure of whether your local content is being recognized as local. It also gives local teams something they never had in the old model: evidence that their concerns are affecting the business. Test in local languages, not just English. An English-only visibility check will not show you what a buyer in Seoul or Madrid is seeing. Consider a composite example drawn from patterns common to global medical device manufacturers. The company has a well-run global site with a dozen market versions. The technical setup, by traditional international SEO standards, is mostly correct, including hreflang and localized URLs. By traditional international SEO standards, it passes. When viewed for geographical signals market by market, the picture is completely different: None of these are translation problems. Each one is a missing piece of local knowledge, and each one was probably raised by someone in that market at some point. The fix follows the factory model: Register the facts by market, mark which content is market-variable, have local teams supply the evidence and the questions, let AI assemble and structure the pages, and measure what AI assistants say in each language afterward. The global content model wasn’t wrong to pursue efficiency. For a long time, local responsiveness at scale was simply too expensive, and search engines, using hreflang, were forgiving enough that translated pages could still compete. AI search removes that forgiveness. When content is the same or very similar everywhere, AI systems collapse them into a single entity, and the strongest version speaks for every market. AI also removes the excuse. The work that made local content expensive (drafting, translating, formatting, structuring) is exactly the work AI does well. What remains for people is the work local teams were asking to do all along. So before you scale your content factory with AI, ask a simple question: Are you using AI to publish more of the same, faster? Or are you using it to give each market what it was asking for, finally? Things are about to get brighter for investors after enduring an extended rough patch in stocks that's seen most of the S&P 500 struggle this year, Morgan Stanley says. Since June 2, the S&P 500 has been flat. The last month has been particularly bumpy for the market, with the benchmark index falling as much as 3% since October 6, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 has lost 9%. Last Friday, selling intensified as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq both plunged amid investor concerns about AI spending, future demand, and earnings uncertainty. But in a client note on Monday, the bank said the downside would soon be over. "Given last week's price action, we think the correction that began in June is now in the final innings," Mike Wilson, the bank's chief investment officer, wrote in the note. But did Allen's off day open the door for a new No. 1? I have more on that — and on Jared Goff, Jayden Daniels, Kyler Murray, Justin Herbert and others — in this week’s QB Stock Market. These aren’t your typical QB rankings. I’m focused on contextualizing the fluctuations of starters' performances throughout the season. I don’t write about every quarterback every week, but I dive deeply into the most compelling performers. No one — not even Josh Allen — is safe at the top. No one — not even Joe Fagnano — is stuck at the bottom. There is room for quick ascent — and rapid decline. One question holds the most importance: What have you done for your team lately? Previous: Offseason | Preseason | Week 1 | Week 2 | Week 3 | Week 4 | Week 5 | Week 6 | Week 7 | Week 8 Previous ranking: N/A Previous ranking: 32 ↑ Previous ranking: 28 ↓ Previous ranking: 29 Now what? For years, Herbert has been a clear-cut solution to the Chargers' problems. He elevated them when they were down. He optimized their talent and offset poor coaching. Now it’s more complicated. He is making two or three terrible throws per game — netting at least one interception per game. And so (while he’s actually solid on most his other throws), his turnovers have been costly.  For the first time in his career, he’s an active participant in the demise of the Chargers' season. He’s a part of the reason why they look like one of the most hopeless franchises — worse even than the Miami Dolphins, who have somehow started to turn things around with a roster that boasts less talent than the Chargers'.  Herbert threw two interceptions this past Sunday, and the first pick was just as awful and inexcusable as the second. There was otherwise plenty to like on his film. (I promise!) But it’s hard to get excited about the things he does well because the turnovers this year have been so harmful. He’s constantly playing from behind, and likely because he’s the only person on the team who can make a play to win it, he is taking too many risks. In turn, he’s making a lot of plays that shoot the Chargers in the foot. In Week 8, the Chargers were competitive with the Rams — until Herbert’s first pick shifted the momentum of the game toward Sean McVay’s squad. What’s most troubling: Herbert is developing bad habits that might be hard to shake in 2027 and beyond. The Chargers are endangering further regression of a QB who basically everyone thought would be elite by now. But the Chargers won’t bench Herbert. That’s just not Jim Harbaugh’s move here — particularly when the backup is DJ Uiagalelei. (Who?) So the other potential step is to fire offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel and return to Harbaugh’s system from the previous two years. But you’d be doing that in the middle of the season when it’s really unlikely to change the 0-7 Chargers' fortunes in 2026. It also would look worse before it looked better. (Take the Broncos as an example: changing playcallers and playbooks in the middle of the season. They got worse for two or three weeks — before improving this week against the Chiefs.) That’s probably the right way to go, and perhaps Harbaugh is considering it, given he was very vague and evasive at his latest postgame press conference when asked about McDaniel’s job security. There’s a good player here. Herbert can still be a really good QB. Previous ranking: 25 ↓ Previous ranking: 24 ↓ Previous ranking: 30 ↑ Previous ranking: 31 ↑ Previous ranking: 20 ↓ Outside of interceptions, you don’t typically see a head coach openly criticize a QB’s mistake.  But that’s what coach Kevin O’Connell did when assessing a failed fourth-down conversion attempt early in the fourth quarter in the Vikings' Week 8 loss to the Lions. O’Connell said Murray waited too long to let loose a pass. The QB’s hesitancy was all the rush needed to get to him. And so when Murray finally threw, the ball fell harmlessly incomplete. The problem isn’t just that Murray missed the crucial throw. It isn’t even necessarily that O’Connell is openly highlighting the mistake. It’s that this mistake has been surprisingly common for the veteran QB since taking over the Vikings offense. And if there was a game where Murray could help carry the Vikings, it should have been against the Lions' defense, which has allowed the most passing yards per game and 10th most points per game. And yet Murray looked bad. Maybe worse than usual. At the end of the second quarter, O’Connell appeared to reset his playcalling to help his QB find a rhythm. They moved to the quick game with easy completions — which Murray badly needed because (even with the stat-padding WR screens and checkdowns), he went into halftime having completed 7 of 15 throws for 86 yards and an interception.  That turnover handed points to the Lions before the half. And it was a throw that Murray should never have attempted, with cornerback D.J. Reed standing with perfect leverage in coverage to defend (or, in this case, catch) the throw. Murray is waiting too long to confirm — rather than throwing with anticipation (which is sort of what Kevin O’Connell’s offense is built upon). He’s missing open receivers and open windows to throw. His best throw — and he had just a few good ones in Week 8 — was a seam route to T.J. Hockenson. You can’t build an offense around that throw. The Kyler Murray experiment was compelling, given his unique talents as a thrower and runner. But so far, Murray’s uniqueness has made for a square-peg-round-hole situation in Minnesota. That was from this past Sunday night against the Eagles when Jayden Daniels finished with a win — yet went just 16 of 29 for 217 yards and one touchdown. His completion percentage over expected (-5.3%) felt generous. The Commanders QB missed open receivers with startling regularity. It’s not the Daniels that we know. Just look at his draft profile from 2024 on NFL.com: "Anticipatory thrower with accuracy and feel for attacking zone windows." Daniels, in fact, was such a good thrower on the move that this was also in there: "Substantially more accurate on rollouts than as a scrambling passer." That’s not the Jayden Daniels of 2026. In Week 8, he was demanding more of his receivers than he ever has with his off-target throws. Consider, too, how many circus catches Chig Okonkwo and Treylon Burks had to make. And those throws were technically "on target." One of the misfires came immediately after Daniels nearly left the game, taking a big hit to the midsection. It makes you wonder whether the attrition of playing QB behind this OL — and taking so many hits — is impacting his ability to deliver the ball with his patented accuracy. The good news is, Daniels’ decision-making has continued to look sharp from down to down. He doesn’t turn the ball over. He avoids sacks when he can. He obviously had a pair of infamously bad moments earlier this year. But he still looks like a QB who knows what he’s looking at — and knows what to do with the ball. So the Commanders need to figure out — urgently — why he seems so scattered as a thrower. Because above all, they must preserve his strengths, even if the staff has too many issues to develop him properly. Previous ranking: 17 ↑ Previous ranking: 15 ↑ Previous ranking: 10 ↓ Previous ranking: 13 ↑ Previous ranking: 11 ↑ Previous ranking: 9 Previous ranking: 4 ↓ Previous ranking: 8 ↑ Previous ranking: 7 ↑ Jared Goff got a signature win. Did he get help from his running back? Of course. Jahmyr Gibbs rushed for 153 yards and a touchdown. Did he get help from his defense? Yes. I did not see them frustrating the Vikings quite like this. But Goff did what he has done all year, which was to facilitate and set up the offense for success. Which sounds kinda boring because it is kinda boring. His stat line wasn’t all that awesome. He was 18 of 25 for 176 passing yards, one touchdown and one interception. Even the advanced stats were … meh. His completion percentage over expected was -1.9%, per Next Gen Stats. But there’s context: The Vikings blitzed on 26 of 29 dropbacks (89.7%) in Week 8. All but three! It was the highest blitz rate by a team since at least 2018, breaking the previous record set by … these Vikings in Week 7. (They blitzed the Colts on 85.2% of dropbacks, per Next Gen Stats.) Despite that, Goff tied the record for completions against the blitz (17) and managed 130 yards, a touchdown and an interception. That’s pretty good, especially because the Vikings’ blitzes are a head-spinning array of concepts that are designed (by the best defensive coordinator in the NFL, Brian Flores) to turn a QB into a shell of himself.  And it didn’t work against Goff. He has the reputation of folding under pressure. He has been worse against the blitz this year than he has been since 2023, with an EPA per dropback of .13 against the blitz, per Next Gen Stats. And I’ve been holding that stat — among others — against him as he’s had an elite season of counting stats: 1,964 passing yards, 15 touchdowns, one interception. But this game went a long way in reassuring me that those counting numbers are largely indicative of how well Goff is playing. His offensive line has been outstanding. His skill players are terrific. And it’s all linked to Goff’s performance. I’ve got to give him credit for a well-managed game against the league’s most intimidating defense. Previous ranking: 1 ↓ Week 8 was not exactly Josh Allen’s finest performance.  Even as the Bills blew out the Ravens (thanks largely to the fact that Baltimore had to play QB3 Joe Fagnano), the final score and stat line don’t totally represent how dysfunctional things were for Buffalo. So while I’d normally roll my eyes at a coach who criticizes his team after a game with a lopsided scoreline, I nodded my head at Joe Brady when he said the following: "I think our standard wasn't good. I thought our execution, our details, penalties, and fumbles — I thought we started off fast in that first drive, but then I felt like we kind of lost our way, in terms of some of the little things." Allen was no exception. He missed receiver Keon Coleman for what would’ve been a long touchdown in the first half. Even on D.J. Moore’s leaping grab in the third quarter, the receiver had to spin backward to make the grab. At multiple points in the game, Allen whipped fastballs into tight areas in hopes that he could sneak them by defenders, but the results were tipped passes and drops. Some of this was a credit to the Ravens' defense. Some of this was Allen allowing a lack of precision — and perhaps even a sense of complacency — into a game where Lamar Jackson exited after one play. I’m not worried about Allen. He’ll be just fine. And after all, he scored three touchdowns (two passing, one rushing). The dude is a machine. But the Bills as a whole are starting to show some weaknesses and vulnerabilities. Allen can and will compensate for those issues, scoring more and more and more for a defense that never seems effective. He did that this past weekend. He’ll probably do that next weekend. But to get to the Super Bowl, I think the Bills' defense will need to get its act together. Previous ranking: 2 ↑ Let’s look back at 2024 for a second. In Week 16, Caleb Williams (then a rookie QB) and the Bears lost, 6-3, to Mike Macdonald (then a rookie head coach) and the Seahawks. Williams looked bad — OK, extremely bad — with 160 passing yards, three sacks and two fumbles (none lost). Now think about what Williams did to Seattle on Monday night. He was 24 of 34 for 247 yards and a touchdown, with just one sack. He operated an offense that looked relentless and, at times, unstoppable. And for all the love for the Seahawks defense (which is deserved) for their high IQ, it was Bears coach Ben Johnson who — with the help of Williams — proved to have the smartest unit in football. They ran quick snaps to expose the Seattle’s disguises. They had a brilliant piece of sequenced playcalling, where they ran up the middle to the 1-yard line, where they yelled that they were going to run the play again — only to … run play-action for an easy touchdown pass.  After that play opened up scoring, Williams had words with his teammates on the sideline. "I don’t give a f--- who they are," Williams said.  Nor should he. Because wolves do not concern themselves with the opinions of sheep. And the Bears apparently do not concern themselves with game plans from the Seahawks. Williams is a destroyer of defensive game plans. For the first time in his career, he is the pro quarterback that he was meant to be. In other words, he is the QB that no one wants to face.

Login  Vlad  03 November 2026   RedMagic Android Announcement  Back in mid-October, the RedMagic 12 Pro+ was unveiled in China, and RedMagic said at the time that it would also launch globally as the RedMagic 12 Pro. Today, the RedMagic 12 Pro is official for the rest of the world, and it keeps the RGB-lit liquid cooling and the 8,400 mAh battery of its Chinese counterpart. That battery is 12% bigger than the 7,500 mAh cell in the RedMagic 11 Pro, yet the new handset is thinner, at 8.5mm (vs. 8.9mm). Charging is where the global model differs from the Chinese one - you get 80W wired charging instead of 120W, along with wireless and bypass charging. The 6.85-inch 1.5K BOE-made X11 OLED screen has what the company says is the industry's first 185Hz refresh rate paired with a 'true full-screen' design with an under-display selfie camera. The panel comes with 0.96mm bezels, reaches 1,900 nits of global peak brightness and 5,000 nits of local peak brightness, and offers an instantaneous touch sampling rate of up to 5,000Hz. Hidden underneath are a ninth-generation 16MP selfie camera developed with BOE and a 3D ultrasonic fingerprint reader. The Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset is at the helm, joined by the in-house RedCore R5 gaming chip and the G1 display chip, with up to 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. On the back, there's a 50MP main camera with OIS and a 50MP ultrawide.     The RedMagic 12 Pro in Nightfreeze The AquaCore Cooling System 3.0 combines the dual-loop liquid cooling, which now lights up in RGB, with a 25,500 RPM fan, a vapor chamber with a 15% larger effective cooling area, and Liquid Metal 4.0. The new micro-pump delivers up to 130kPa of output pressure, 85% more than its predecessor's, while drawing as little as 20mW. The phone is IP68/IP69-rated for dust and water resistance, while the fan area carries a separate IPX8 rating. You also get 520Hz shoulder triggers (the Chinese model's are rated at 700Hz), stereo speakers with Dolby Atmos, an X-axis linear motor, an IR blaster, NFC, Wi-Fi 7, and a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port. It runs RedMagic OS 12 based on Android 17, with Gemini integration, PC game emulation, and Steam access through the X-Gravity gaming center.     The RedMagic 12 Pro in Subzero The RedMagic 12 Pro comes in Nightfreeze (transparent black) and Subzero (transparent silver) color options. Here's a handy table with pricing information for all possible versions. Author of the AI Insider newsletter Chinese AI models have fallen sharply behind American rivals in a closely watched ranking, raising fresh questions about whether the threat from cheaper, freely available AI technology has been exaggerated. Artificial Analysis, a prominent independent firm that measures AI performance, recently overhauled its testing system to better reflect how people actually use the technology. One crucial change: Many of the tests are now kept secret, making it harder for AI companies to train their models specifically to perform well on them. The results were striking. Artificial Analysis said the best so-called open-weight AI models had trailed the overall leader by just three points under the previous system. Under the new system, that gap widened to 12 points. The 12-point gap included Moonshot's Kimi K3.1 Pro. Among models with publicly released weights, the leaders scored just 32 points, compared with 58 for the then overall leader, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5. The findings could have major implications for the AI industry and the billions of dollars investors are pouring into it. Chinese companies have been releasing powerful AI models that other businesses can download and adapt, often at lower costs than American alternatives. This fueled concern that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic could struggle to charge premium prices for their proprietary technology. The new rankings suggest that threat may have been overstated, potentially strengthening the investment case for Anthropic's planned IPO and a possible future OpenAI listing. Sridhar Ramaswamy, CEO of Snowflake and a former Google executive, highlighted the significance of the testing change. "The day benchmarks went private, the open-model gap went from 3 points to 12," he wrote on X. "Were open models catching up, or was the test leaking?" His point: When AI companies know exactly how their technology will be tested, they can train it to excel at those particular tasks. That doesn't necessarily mean their models perform equally well in the real world. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and other AI experts have called this "benchmark hacking." Keeping the tests secret makes these hacks harder. The new results suggest American companies have a bigger lead than previously believed, particularly in complex scientific tasks. Even Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller Anthropic model, outperformed every AI model with publicly released weights. Even proponents of open-weight models admitted something has likely been awry. "I do think the previous index was flattering the open weight models too strongly," said Nathan Lambert, cofounder of Trillium Labs, which researches large language models, especially open-weight models. There's another reason to question the threat from open-weight AI models: How much are people actually using them? Dax Raad, cofounder of software development company OpenCode, recently examined traffic through OpenRouter, a popular service that lets developers access AI models from different providers. He estimated that almost all the previous day's DeepSeek traffic flowing through OpenRouter could be handled by a single rack of powerful Nvidia computers, costing roughly $6 million to $7 million. That's a surprisingly small amount of computing power given the enormous attention Chinese AI models have attracted. OpenRouter represents only a slice of the market, so its figures don't capture all demand for open-weight models. But Raad's broader point is important: Much of the industry's enormous AI infrastructure investment is being driven by major providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, rather than the smaller developers using open models. Consider the more than 1 billion people who use ChatGPT every month. These folks are using OpenAI's closed AI models all the time — potentially way more activity than is captured by AI gateway services such as OpenRouter. Together, the rankings and usage figures raise two questions about open-weight AI: Is it really as good as the leading American technology, and is demand as substantial as the hype suggests? There are important caveats. Trillium's Lambert said open-weight models remain highly competitive in areas such as software development, and can offer businesses greater control and potentially lower costs. Still, the new evidence challenges a powerful narrative that has shaped the industry: that Chinese AI companies are rapidly catching America's leaders and threatening their business models. For investors weighing the enormous valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic, that distinction matters enormously. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here.
