Cool Hunting®                Visit tastemaker-approved locations within a twenty minute walk from the property like we did in Tokyo’s Ginza district with Ryo Takashima There is a distinct art to navigating a metropolis on foot. In an era of packed itineraries and endless saved lists, the most meaningful urban discoveries often happen within a tightly bounded radius, and AC Hotels by Marriott’s new AC 20-Minute Edit series turns that idea into a guide, mapping cultural, culinary, art and fashion destinations within a 20-minute walk of each hotel. The series launches at eight AC Hotels locations—Tokyo, Melbourne, Montreal, Portland (Maine), Naples (Florida), Lima, Glasgow and Krakow—with each market teaming up with local creators, chefs, designers and cultural curators who embody the design-forward ethos of their respective cities. We experienced this firsthand in Tokyo, spending time with Ryo Takashima, founder and fashion director of the retailer +81 and founder and creative director of the minimalist label Clesste. His popular Instagram shares his passion for Japanese fashion and creative culture. He took us to some of his favorite spots near the AC Hotel Tokyo Ginza, which sits amid some of the city’s best shopping, and many of them also appear on our own list of Ginza favorites. We stay at the AC Hotel Tokyo Ginza often, and AC Hotels are always on our list when we’re paying our own way at CH or traveling personally. They’re nearly always in central neighborhoods, with simple, modern and considered design, and they offer what we typically need while skipping the things we don’t need or have to pay for. Rooms are usually just the right size—comfortable and not claustrophobic, though rarely large (the Ginza location’s Superior rooms are larger for a modest bump in rate). If a trip is mostly work or mostly out and about, and you want to be comfortable and productive in between, they’re well worth a look. Takashima’s Tokyo 20-Minute Edit selections (all within a 20-minute walk of the hotel): Dover Street Market Ginza Known to every CH reader with any interest in fashion, DSM is a fixture on our itineraries, and visitors to Tokyo are welcomed by the company’s largest shop in the world: six floors of avant-garde garb, art installations, books and more. Rose Bakery makes a welcome pit stop for coffee and a quick snack, and the store’s selection of Porter bags is consistently on point. Ginza Six Tokyo Recognized for its striking facade designed by Yoshio Taniguchi and the art installations that fill its interior atrium, Ginza Six houses top-tier design houses, luxury fashion boutiques and a rooftop garden with panoramic views of the Tokyo skyline. Alongside global luxury brands, the mall carries Japanese labels including Evisu, Jotaro Saito and and wander, plus plenty of snack and dining options. The Tokyo Ginza Boutique Selected by Takashima for its refined approach to retail, this destination highlights contemporary tailoring, understated luxury and meticulous Japanese craftsmanship that directly mirror his minimalist design aesthetic. Ginza Sony Park Gallery An experimental public space and gallery that reopened in 2025 after a substantial renovation, Ginza Sony Park mixes technology, music, media art and urban landscape architecture with an impressive calendar of events. It offers an ever-changing, interactive glimpse into Japan’s visual culture. Barneys New York Ginza New York’s go-to department store lives on in Japan (and in Seoul as Barneys New York Beauty), though none of these outposts are owned by the original entity. The Ginza location will feel familiar to anyone who has visited a Barneys, with a well-curated selection of international fashion designers, fine jewelry and modern lifestyle goods in a sleek, sophisticated environment. We couldn’t not add a few of our own neighborhood favorites to explore on your next visit to Ginza. The 280-year-old Kuboki Tatami offers tasteful tatami accessories including placemats, coasters and one of our new obsessions: tatami phone mats.  Founded in 1948, Sakura Seisakusho makes iconic midcentury modern furniture, including George Nakashima’s designs. Whether you’re shopping or just browsing, it’s a block away from the AC Hotel Tokyo Ginza and absolutely worth a visit. Hungry after all that shopping? Nair’s Restaurant, the oldest authentic Indian restaurant in Japan, is just steps from the hotel. The small, very casual joint is known for its Murgi Lunch: spiced chicken curry—deboned at your table—served with mashed potatoes, boiled cabbage and rice. There’s nearly always a line, and it’s worth the wait. Whether it’s before your day gets started or upon your return, you can enjoy breakfast or a casual meal at the AC Kitchen and Lounge on the ground floor or have a drink at the bar. And on your way up to your room with all of your duty-free goods, pick up one of the brand’s signature Lavender Turndown sachets to keep the mood mellow. Four planned "hyperscale" data centres are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs The UK government's ambition of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 could be undermined by its new deal on AI data centres, according to BBC research. During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said data centres would be allowed to build onsite power generation while they wait for a grid connection. BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four planned "hyperscale" data centres - including three in the south of England -  are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs, creating more CO2 than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined. Labour MP Toby Perkins, who chairs the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said a substantial increase in the use of natural gas "can't be the future". "Government absolutely shouldn't be in the business of just saying anyone who wants to bring it here, can do whatever you like to power it, because that is not acceptable," he said. Toby Perkins MP, chair of the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said the use of gas power for AI data centres was "not acceptable" The government said data centres were "essential to Britain's economy" and that its new Data Centre Covenant set clear expectations for developers to pay a fair share of the costs they impose on the energy system and deliver benefits for local communities. Data centres are warehouses full of powerful computer servers used to run a vast range of digital services, including streaming, banking and public services and have been part of the British landscape for more than two decades. But a new generation of data centres due to come on stream in the next few years will operate on a much larger scale to cope with the growing computing demand needed for increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence technology. They will consume considerably more energy than their predecessors at a time when the National Grid is already struggling to meet demand. Ofgem, the energy market regulator, says data centre developers are seeking connections totalling 72 gigawatts. The peak electricity demand across the whole country last year was 45 gigawatts. There are plans to construct an AI data centre on the the site surrounding Redcar's former blast furnace  Such is the demand for access to the already under-strain national electricity grid, some data centre developers have been told they could be waiting up to 10 years for the system to be upgraded to provide them with a connection. Nathan MacWhinnie, head of market intelligence and oversight at Ofgem, said: "In a lot of places, the grid is at capacity. I think sometimes it's easy to forget the scale of the demand of these connections. These projects are sometimes the size of cities." In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a British Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in return for priority grid connections. But he also said that where grid connections were unavailable, developers would be permitted to generate their own power on-site. BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four data centres are already looking at using gas-fired power stations to meet their electricity needs. If continuously running at full capacity, our calculations show they would require 1.3 gigawatts of power and could produce an estimated 4.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions a year. This could be more than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined. Oliver Hayes, of environmental charity Global Action Plan, is concerned about the use of gas-fired power to supply data centres with electricity Oliver Hayes, head of campaigns at environmental charity Global Action Plan, said: "If we're powering by gas that means local communities are going to have huge gas turbines on their doorstep, and they are going to be generating a huge amount of local air pollution and a huge amount of noise and they will be using a huge amount of water from the local water supply." The developments already considering on-site gas vary in scale. At Acre Slough, west of London, developers say they could use gas engines with a generating capacity of up to 49.5 megawatts while waiting for a National Grid connection, something they expect could take at least 10 years. At Wapsey's Wood, next to the M40 in Buckinghamshire, a proposed 200-megawatt gas power station could operate until sufficient grid capacity becomes available, currently not expected until 2040. "It would be a disaster for us environmentally," said Buckinghamshire independent councillor Ed Gemmell, who also leads the Climate Party. "If allowed, it sets a precedent that we could be getting gas-fired power stations all over the country and that would make it extremely difficult for us to hit any of our environmental and net zero targets." Is it time to press pause on AI data centres? An increasing number of large AI data centres are waiting in the UK energy supply queue - but will meeting that demand derail the road to net zero? 3 November Quest Park has proposed building a data centre on the site of a quarry pit next to the planned Universal theme park in Bedfordshire. It would have a power load - the total amount of electrical power drawn at any given time - of 1 gigawatt, the equivalent to 200,000â250,000 average UK homes. David Kohler, director of Quest Park, has previously told the BBC the company's energy mix was still a "work in progress" and that incorporating renewable power was "sensible" but had to be "feasible". He said creating 1 gigawatt of solar electricity would require an area equivalent to 15% of Bedfordshire, and that wind power was "intermittent and expensive". He said the company was considering alternative technologies that did not rely on gas combustion. In Cardiff, a data centre developer is also seeking permission to build a temporary energy centre that has turbines with a maximum generating capacity of 49.9 megawatts.  Planning documents say it could operate for up to five years if the site cannot secure an electricity grid connection quickly enough. Developer Curtis Hall has described the turbine plan as a "worst-case scenario". Quest Park wants to build a data centre on the site of a quarry pit All four projects say they intend to connect to the national grid when it can meet their electricity needs, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels. The government said its priority was connecting data centres to the grid so they could benefit from the UK's rapidly decarbonising power sector.  It said any behind-the-meter power generation would be tightly controlled, time-limited and allowed only for exceptionally strategic projects where sufficient capacity could not be secured by other means. A government spokesperson added: "Data centres are essential to Britain's economy, supporting everything from online banking to NHS services.  "Pausing development would send jobs, investment and data overseas and leave us more reliant on other countries for critical digital infrastructure. That's why we're backing their growth while making sure it's done responsibly. "Our new Data Centre Covenant sets clear expectations for developers to minimise water use, pay their fair share of energy costs and deliver benefits for local communities." This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Alex Greenberg, an American founder living in Chengdu, China, who runs Observed Media, a creative studio. He is also the creator of the Instagram account @shanghaiobserved. His words have been edited for length and clarity. As graduation from college in Vermont approached, I had no idea what I wanted to do with my life. I'd studied abroad in Australia during my junior year and knew I loved traveling, but I drew a blank on what to do next. Then, in November of my senior year, I received an offer to teach skateboarding in Shanghai. It was my only job offer; I hadn't applied to much else. Teaching skateboarding in China wasn't exactly what I pictured doing with a college degree, but I figured it would make for an interesting gap year. I arrived in January 2015 speaking zero Chinese. More than a decade later, China has shaped my career. Shanghai had become a magnet for street skaters, and most of my friends came through skateboarding and the video production world. It was one of the best social periods of my life. I remember constantly thinking, "What am I doing? This is wild." I'd chosen this completely unexpected life, and somehow it was working. After my one-year contract ended, I expected to go home. But by then, I'd built a network and a life in Shanghai. Leaving didn't make sense. I also had the safety net of teaching English. The US job market felt like a mystery to navigate, so I stayed. Career-wise, I was throwing everything at the wall. I started juggling English teaching and private skate lessons. At the same time, I started Shanghai Observed on Instagram as a daily photography project for fun. There wasn't some grand business plan behind it; I was just walking around Shanghai and documenting the city. In 2016, I got an internship at PUSH Media and eventually worked my way up to project manager. We produced campaigns and events for brands like Adidas, Vans, and The North Face. Meanwhile, Shanghai Observed continued to grow alongside my career. Today, it has over 280,000 followers and gets millions of views a month, mostly from people outside China who are curious about everyday life. It's never been my primary source of income; it's always been more of a passion project. But it opened a lot of doors. I flew to the US for Christmas in December 2019 and planned to return after Chinese New Year. Then COVID hit, and I couldn't get back. I spent about 15 months living with my parents in New York. After that, I went to Kauai to work on a pineapple farm. I was only supposed to be there for three months. China still hadn't reopened, so I stayed in Hawaii for two years. I converted a school bus into a tiny home on a friend's farm, worked as a drone pilot, and spent my free time surfing, playing poker and casual baseball games, and having dinner at friends' houses. Then, in 2023, I moved to San Diego for a remote brand manager role. I had built an entirely different life and career in the US, but China never really disappeared from either, and I continued running the Instagram account. By the end of my time in California, I was paying $2,400 a month in rent, including utilities, for a small one-bedroom place in Encinitas. I loved living near the ocean, but I started thinking about what the same money could buy me elsewhere. I realized I could base myself in China again, build my own media business, and have considerably more money left over to travel. This September, I finally moved back — but instead of returning to Shanghai, I chose Chengdu, a major city in southwestern China. Despite not having lived there before, I had friends there, the creative scene seemed exciting, and it's a much more affordable place to build my business and study Chinese. Shanghai has more opportunity, but also more competition. Chengdu's pace feels slower. The city prides itself on tea houses, long dinners, and relaxing. There's a real emphasis on quality of life and comfort. Right now, I pay 3,000 Chinese yuan, or $420 a month, for a furnished studio on a month-to-month lease. A bowl of noodles costs around $2, and a coffee costs $1.50. I'm producing stories for brands and creators. Shanghai Observed was where I learned how to do it; Observed Media brings it all under one roof. The thread connecting everything I've done — from skateboarding and sharing day-to-day life content in Shanghai to my days in California — has been paying attention to culture and turning it into stories people want to watch. Shanghai Observed is still where I experiment. It's a mix of my own photography and footage, submissions from followers, and content I discover through WeChat groups. When I first moved to Shanghai at 22, I thought I was taking a one-year skateboarding job while I figured out what I wanted to do next. Instead, that spontaneous decision shaped my friendships, my career, the business I'm building, and the way I see the world. More than a decade later, I'm 34 and back in China, starting another chapter. And, strangely enough, I have that same feeling I had when I first arrived: What am I doing? This is wild. Only this time, I have a much better idea of what I'm doing here. Jump to

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus. Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” … Bloomberg’s Dave Lee didn’t hold back. Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions. Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect? Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company. In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away. Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism. Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points. It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Trading volume exceeded 150 million shares, more than triple the daily average, according to market data. Intel's plunge came as Amazon and other technology companies reported quarterly results that deepened investor anxiety over the cost of the artificial intelligence buildout [2]. The decline marked Intel's most severe one-day percentage drop in roughly five decades. NDTV Profit reported the shares were down 29.89% at $64.49 as of 1:26 p.m.Market Reaction and Sector Impact The drop contributed to a broader decline in semiconductor stocks. Intel's decline was steeper than peers, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index falling 5% the same day, according to exchange data. The selloff extended across the technology sector as investors reassessed growth expectations for chipmakers following a round of quarterly earnings. Analysts attributed the selloff to disappointing earnings and concerns over AI spending. "The market is reassessing growth expectations for chipmakers," said an analyst. The report stated that the reaction reflected worries that the massive capital expenditures directed at artificial intelligence infrastructure may not translate into near-term demand for Intel's products. The broader market also felt the impact.Earnings Report and AI Spending Concerns Intel reported quarterly revenue of $13.2 billion, below consensus estimates of $14.5 billion, according to the earnings release. The company lowered its guidance for the next quarter, citing uncertain demand and competitive pressures. The guidance also reflected competitive pressures in the semiconductor industry, where rivals have gained ground in AI-related chips. Amazon and other big tech firms signaled increased capital expenditures on AI infrastructure, raising questions about chip demand, according to CNBC. "We are navigating a dynamic environment and remain focused on our long-term strategy," said Intel's chief financial officer. The combination of soft PC demand and uncertain AI spending plans among major customers contributed to the downward revision in guidance.Government Stake in Intel The stake was valued at approximately $30 billion before the drop, officials said. The investment was intended to support domestic semiconductor production and reduce reliance on foreign chip manufacturing. The $12 billion loss represents a 40% decline in the stake's value, according to calculations based on government filings. Officials said the government remains a long-term investor and the stake is intended to support domestic semiconductor production. The loss comes as the administration has prioritized rebuilding American chip manufacturing capacity. Intel has been a central recipient of federal support aimed at expanding U.S.-based fabrication.Outlook and Analyst Perspectives Analysts remain divided on Intel's near-term prospects, according to research notes. Some cited the company's foundry strategy as a potential long-term positive, while others pointed to competitive pressures from AMD and Nvidia. The divergence in views reflects uncertainty about whether Intel can regain market share in a sector increasingly dominated by AI-focused chipmakers. "The volatility is likely to continue until there is more clarity on AI spending and demand," said Mark Johnson, an analyst. The report stated that Intel's stock is down 60% year-to-date, according to market data. Intel's historical role in the semiconductor industry has made its performance a bellwether for the sector. Watch CBS News  November 3, 2026 / 1:26 PM EST             / CBS News            The midterm elections could reshape Congress as lawmakers grapple with persistent inflation, high energy prices and rising fiscal debt. For investors, by contrast, the political outcome could deliver a boost.  Data from financial firm Edward Jones shows that the S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970. In the six months following midterm elections, S&P returns averaged 15.5%. "Volatility around the vote is possible, but markets have historically performed well in the year following midterms as political uncertainty recedes and attention returns to the economic outlook," Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at the global investment firm Principal Asset Management, said in an email on Tuesday as Americans cast their votes.  With congressional control in the balance, Wall Street analysts are also considering the impact divided government could have on stocks if the Democrats win the House, Senate or both chambers. Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to analysts.  "Less change makes a more predictable environment, which allows companies to invest in longer-term projects," Chris Low, chief economist at FHN Financial, a capital markets firm, said in an email Tuesday. "That tends to be good for earnings."  Less stock market volatility doesn't guarantee investors an easy ride, however. Gridlock in Washington, D.C., could also fuel another partisan standoff on the nation's debt, which recently surpassed $40 trillion, or spur the U.S. government to increase its borrowing to fund its priorities, according to economists. That could unnerve bond investors, who are worried that Washington is on an unsustainable fiscal trajectory, Ed Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, said in a note to investors. "Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations," he said. The Bipartisan Policy Center, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, estimates that the U.S. will reach the debt limit again sometime between late winter and midsummer of 2027. At that point, lawmakers will have to decide whether to raise the debt ceiling, temporarily suspend it or risk another government shutdown. Volatility could also persist if President Trump continues to rely on his executive authority to accomplish his priorities, Yardeni said. In that case, Democrats would have little power to restrain Mr. Trump even if they controlled Congress, he noted. "Hence, a blue wave could deliver a cold shower for stocks, though we would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the remarkable strength of the economy and corporate earnings," Yardeni said. A Democratic sweep could have other implications for the economy beyond financial markets. That could include Democrats blocking Trump-appointed regulators, according to Jaret Seiberg, a financial policy analyst and managing director at investment bank TD Cowen. "They [could] leverage this power to force the President to fill Democratic seats on independent agencies like the FDIC, SEC and CFTC," he said. A Democratic majority in the Senate would also elevate Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, to head the Senate Banking Committee, giving her more latitude to pass populist legislation, Seiberg added. Warren would replace South Carolina Republican Sen. Tim Scott, who currently chairs the influential panel.  However, lawmakers would still be restricted in what they can do at a federal level, given the president's ability to veto legislation, UBS analysts said in a research note.         Edited by                                                                            Alain  Sherter  In:        © 2026 CBS Interactive Inc. Login  Vlad  03 November 2026   Apple iOS  Apple's first foldable, the iPhone Duo, sold out within hours of pre-orders opening on October 16, and shipping dates quickly slipped all the way to January. Ahead of launch day, the company also warned of limited walk-in stock in its stores. Now, if you were hoping things would get better soon, Apple's CEO has some bad news for you. Speaking yesterday, after Apple reported record results for its September quarter, John Ternus said the Duo "is constrained as of today". He added that the production ramp is going well, but that the company can't predict when supply and demand will be in balance. COO Sabih Khan gave analysts practically the same answer on the earnings call, saying it's "really hard to predict" when that will happen. So if you order an iPhone Duo from Apple today, you're looking at a delivery estimate in January, and stores have had little stock available for online reservations. That's despite Apple reportedly ordering 44% more units from its suppliers last month. Ternus also addressed the inner display damage some early buyers have run into. He said "a very small percentage" of units have been returned for display issues and that Apple is replacing them. That's in line with what the company said last week, when it pointed affected users to AppleCare. The September quarter results don't include any Duo sales, since the device only went on sale on October 23. For the current quarter, which covers the holidays, Apple expects revenue to grow between 7% and 10%, a forecast CFO Kevan Parekh says reflects the company's "best view of constrained supply". Gold is barreling toward its worst year in over a decade. The correction in AI stocks has sucked up investors' attention lately, but it's overshadowed a quiet, dramatic move in gold prices this year. The yellow metal, which was one of the hottest investments in 2025, is down about 29% from its January high, trading below $4,000 an ounce on Tuesday.  The whipsaw is the result of a few things plaguing the US economy and markets this year, from higher rates to a panicked risk-off move in stocks. Gold is now down 9% for the year — putting it on track for its worst annual performance in 11 years, when it plunged around 10% in 2015. The precious metal also dropped more than 3% in October, marking its worst October since the Great Financial Crisis, according to an analysis from economist David Rosenberg. It's unusual for gold to sell-off in tandem with stocks. The safe haven is thought to slowly appreciate and provide a safe haven when stocks are volatile or when markets get rocked by geopolitical events. Demand for gold also generally picks up when inflation fears are on the rise, as investors see it as a hedge against a devalued fiat currency, but that hasn't proven true in 2026 either, even as the Iran war causes oil and gas prices to spike.  "Gold is now behaving in too much of a bizarre and unpredictable pattern, and traditional correlations have broken down," Rosenberg wrote this week. "Gold is increasingly behaving like a risk asset, which is an entirely new dynamic." So, what gives? There are a few unusual reasons the precious metal has continued to slide this year, even amid circumstances that would normally stoke a rally. Here's what's been driving the decline — and what it says about the US economy and markets, according to analysts. While fears of hotter inflation have normally boosted gold prices, higher rate expectations lift Treasury yields and the value of the US dollar, two safe-havens that compete with gold for capital.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Treasury yields are elevated across maturity curve, attesting to ongoing fears about the US fiscal outlook and higher inflation overall. The benchmark 10-year US Treasury yield was around 4.91% on Tuesday, up 77 basis points year-to-date. The weakness in gold also reflects investors' bullishness for the greenback, Rosenberg said, attesting to how markets are focused on the expectation for higher interest rates. The US Dollar Index, which weighs the dollar's value against a basket of other major currencies, ticked up to 101 on Tuesday, up 3% since the start of the year. What it says about the economy: Higher interest rates are the big story. That's increased the opportunity cost of holding gold, while a stronger US dollar has made it more expensive for international buyers to purchase bullion, Adam Perry, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said. The Fed put its rate-hiking cycle on pause at its last policy meeting, but investors expect the central bank to resume tightening heading into 2027. Markets are now pricing in a 75% probability the Fed will raise rates another quarter of a percentage point before the end of the year, and a 21% probability that will be followed by another quarter-point hike in January. Central banks continue to be major buyers of gold as they diversify their reserves, but demand from other segments is fading. Much of the decline was fueled by people purchasing less physical gold and gold jewelry, the World Gold Council said, noting that bar and coin demand has fallen 19% year-over-year, while global jewelry demand is down 17%. In the US, gold jewelry revenue is up overall, but unit sales have declined. Gold jewelry growth is concentrated at "higher price points," though "lower-priced merchandise" is underperforming, according to a September report from the analytics firm Tenoris. What it says about the economy: The K-shaped economy may be playing a role in gold's decline this year, with more aspirational luxury shoppers pulling back on gold purchases as inflation curtails spending. A worldwide slowdown in jewelry and luxury goods may also be a factor, particularly as consumers in the US and China rein in spending overall. "Whether described as a K-shaped economy, market bifurcation, or a shift in the composition of consumer spending, the data point to a jewelry market increasingly divided by price point," Tenoris wrote in its monthly report. Gold's decline is largely a rates story, but consumers pulling back certainly "can move the needle," Jose Torres, a senior economist at Interactive Brokers, told Business Insider. "I think it's been that combination of forces," he said. Investors may be looking to sell gold to build up more cash on the sidelines, according to Perry. It's a testament to how negative investor sentiment has been lately, given the brutal losses in the AI trade, with the Nasdaq 100 slipping into an official correction and shedding around $2 trillion in market cap since hitting a record in early October.  "This helps explain why gold fell sharply alongside equities on Friday, despite heightened uncertainty," Perry wrote in a note to clients. Margin calls on tech positions may also have forced investors to sell gold lately, Rosenberg said, noting that those trading on margin may receive calls from their brokerages asking them to deposit more cash to backstop losses on their stock holdings. Debit balances in customers' margin accounts sat near a record high in October, FINRA data shows.  What it says about markets: Risk-off sentiment may be so extreme that investors are selling gold instead of using it as a safe haven. "Investors liquidating other assets in the process… if you recall, we saw this take hold briefly in the fall of 2008 and after the 9/11 terrorist attacks as well," Rosenberg said. Investors were also highly exposed to gold after its meme-like rally in 2025, Torres noted. Gold has historically seen large upswings before entering a period of near-zero gains, Torres said. He pointed to the metal's double-digit rally in 2025, which mirrored gold's explosive rally coming out of the Great Financial Crisis. The metal stagnated for the following decade before seeing a similar run-up, he noted.  Gold may be entering a similar yearslong technical holding pattern with subdued gains, Torres said, adding that investors may be more focused on other assets, like stocks and real estate, for stronger returns. "If you just generally don't have the investor demand, then it can't really rally," he said of the outlook for gold.  Get the latest Gold price here. Jump to

The session marked one of the largest one-day declines in recent months. The retreat followed weaker-than-expected corporate earnings and cautious guidance from several large technology companies, market participants said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 also closed lower, though the heaviest losses were concentrated in AI-linked names.Market Move and Immediate Triggers Semiconductor and cloud-computing shares fell after quarterly results missed some analyst estimates, according to company filings and analyst notes. Investors reduced positions in companies tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure, citing uncertainty over capital spending and profit timelines. Losses were pushed in part by Amazon, which shed about 2% when trading opened Friday morning, according to a market recap [1]. Treasury yields and volatility measures rose as investors moved toward assets viewed as safer, exchange data showed. Officials did not comment on the decline. The CBOE Volatility Index, a gauge of expected stock market turbulence, climbed during the session. The pullback extended to a range of AI-adjacent companies, from chipmakers to data-center operators. Analysts described the selling as orderly but broad, with investors trimming exposure rather than abandoning the sector outright. The move followed a period of rapid gains that had pushed several AI-linked stocks to record highs earlier in the year.Earnings Reports Put AI Spending Under Scrutiny Several large technology firms reported increased AI-related capital expenditures while offering limited near-term revenue forecasts, according to earnings statements. Amazon's capital expenditures for 2026 ballooned to $220 billion, according to the recap [1]. The figure underscored concerns that spending on AI infrastructure is outpacing the revenue it generates. Analysts said investors are questioning whether current valuations reflect expected AI profits. One portfolio manager said, "The market is repricing the assumption that AI spending will produce immediate returns," according to a note distributed to clients. The comment reflected a broader shift in sentiment as earnings reports failed to deliver the payoff some investors had anticipated. A company executive said demand for AI computing remains strong but supply constraints and costs affect margins, according to remarks on an earnings call. The executive's comments highlighted the tension between robust demand and the expense of building the infrastructure to meet it. Booking Holdings took a $900 million revenue reduction and accrued a $100 million loss in the third quarter tied to a potential Federal Trade Commission complaint against its Priceline brand, which the company said is in discussions with the FTC to resolve. In a quarterly filing Tuesday, Booking said the FTC may seek restitution and penalties exceeding $1 billion, plus litigation and similar claims in other jurisdictions, and that litigation remains possible. The company disclosed in the second quarter that the FTC intended to file a complaint against Priceline and a B2B affiliate partner over disclosures, fees, customer support, and billing practices; Reuters reported last month, citing anonymous sources, that the partner is Guest Reservations. The FTC matter runs alongside a European Commission investigation that has called Booking.com's practices for combating fake listings and phishing "substandard." Operationally, net income fell 1% to $2.7 billion on revenue of $8.9 billion, also down 1%, while room nights rose 7%, accelerating from 5% in the second quarter. CFO Ewout Steenbergen described the fourth-quarter travel environment as "mixed," with moderation in international demand and domestic travel holding up as travelers take shorter trips closer to home. Connected trip transactions — bookings across two or more verticals — grew almost 20% year over year and made up a low double-digit share of Booking.com transactions.

Anthropic has confirmed in a recent S-1 filing that it spent $1.711 billion on personnel in its most recent three-month period, down slightly on the previous quarter's $1.857 billion but up around 3.5x compared with the same quarter in 2025 ($489 million). With around 5,300 people on the books, it means the average worker set the company back over $322,000 for the quarter, or over $107,000 per month. While these figures are likely wild overestimates for the average worker's pay, they show just how much the AI giant is having to spend on talent compared with last year. Crucially, the average worker did not receive $107,000 in a single month, because these figures also include bonuses, employee benefits, payroll taxes and stock-based compensation. An estimated $1.1 billion of the quarterly total came from stock-based compensation, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the total sum. Still, personnel costs accounted for around 15% of the company's revenue over the first nine months of 2026, which puts Anthropic in a positive position. The company spent $4.8 billion on personnel in the first three quarters. Flip those figures around and we have a company that's making an estimated $6.6 million in revenue per employee, compared with $3.2 million at Meta and $2.5 million at Google, per Business Insider calculations. Anthropic doesn't publish salary information, but given its huge expenditure relative to the number of employees, it's clear that recruiting AI talent is expensive. With stock-based compensation accounting for two-thirds of Anthropic's personnel expenditure, workers are likely being attracted by the potential of huge future wealth, rather than immediate compensation. Decision Engine Trackers Event Intelligence News Podcasts and Videos Events Publications Services Photo Caption: Skift Transatlantic Summit 2026 - Dublin, Ireland                    At the Skift Transatlantic Summit, Tourism Ireland Chief Executive Alice Mansergh explained how the island of Ireland is navigating current headwinds by investing in connectivity marketing, market diversification, AI-driven discovery, and the authentic local experiences that can keep the country high on travelers’ wish lists.             This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner. North America remains one of Ireland’s most valuable visitor markets, but the outlook is getting more complicated. At the Skift Transatlantic Summit, Tourism Ireland Chief Executive Alice Mansergh pointed to continued growth alongside signs of softening demand as travelers contend with higher costs and economic uncertainty. So far in 2026, Ireland has welcomed 5% more visitors from North America, with spending up 10%. But Mansergh said the past few months have been softer, as travelers think more carefully about their finances and increasingly seek flexible or refundable bookings. “For all of us, it becomes really important to be at the top of the travel wishlist,” she said.  That challenge is shaping Tourism Ireland’s marketing strategy. Its new “Ireland Goes Beyond” campaign highlights the scenery, culture, heritage, and local experiences that make Ireland worth choosing, even as travelers become more selective about where they spend.                          Growth in a World Reordered                     Staying on travelers’ wish lists is only part of the challenge. Ireland also needs to maintain the air connections that bring those travelers to the destination. With jet fuel costs up sharply and fewer Europeans traveling to the U.S., Mansergh said airlines are looking more closely at which transatlantic routes remain profitable. Tourism Ireland works with carriers to promote strategic routes and stimulate inbound demand. Mansergh summed up the immediate challenge simply: “fill the planes to keep the planes.” Healthy two-way travel matters, she added, because weaker outbound traffic from Europe can put the same routes that bring North American visitors to Ireland under pressure. “When you lose the connectivity, that can be damaging,” she said.  Those pressures reinforce the importance of a diversified visitor base. North America generates just over a third of Ireland’s inbound overseas revenue, with Europe contributing roughly another third. Britain offers another opportunity, with visitors from Ireland’s nearest neighbor twice as likely to return. “Now is not the time to be wholly dependent on just one market or another,” Mansergh said.  Beyond traditional marketing and airline partnerships, Tourism Ireland is also adapting to how travelers discover destinations. Its research found that the number of people naming AI as their primary source of travel inspiration has doubled in the past year. The organization is responding by optimizing its digital content for generative AI. According to Mansergh, information provided by Tourism Ireland now contributes to answers for 19% of queries about the destination across tools including ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. The goal is to influence which experiences AI recommends, particularly lesser-known attractions and local businesses that might otherwise be overlooked. But visibility in AI search also depends on what travelers are seeing and saying about a destination across the web. “Choose what you want to be famous for,” Mansergh said. Tourism Ireland has applied that thinking to Halloween, building awareness of the holiday’s roots in the ancient Irish festival of Samhain through its own content and platforms such as Reddit, YouTube, and Tripadvisor. “You need a bit of a surround sound of people talking about the things you want them to be talking about,” she said. Technology may be changing how travelers discover Ireland, but the experiences that attract them often have little to do with technology. “For me, I always want AI to stand for, yes, artificial intelligence, but also authentic Ireland,” she said. She pointed to sheepdog demonstrations, cider-making farms, and traditional currach-building as examples of experiences that bring travelers closer to local culture while spreading tourism to more regions. “The more digital we are,” Mansergh said, “the more we crave those authentic touch and feel real moments.”  For 2027, Tourism Ireland plans to keep focusing on connectivity, year-round travel, and emerging opportunities such as “cool-cations.” Taken together, those priorities reflect Tourism Ireland’s approach to a more uncertain market: Protect the connections that bring visitors to Ireland, reach travelers through new channels, and give them compelling reasons to visit. Is it cheaper to build your own speaker? For audiophiles who have a workshop setup, know a thing or two about wiring, and want to emulate mid- to high-end speakers, sure, it's a great project to take on. But for a budget entry-level speaker under $100, or speakers that are small enough to fit under a PC monitor, it's not worth it. Mass-market manufacturing supply chains are nearly impossible to beat on price alone, making a DIY build in this bracket hard to justify. But at the mid-range to flagship level, a DIY build is well worth the time and energy, not to mention the financial savings compared to pre-assembled commercial speakers. For example, assembling a high-quality component kit like a $400 parts pack from GR-Research can deliver audio quality comparable to commercial speakers costing $1,000 or more. At the high end, DIY builders can make world-class speakers for a fraction of retail pricing by using top-tier component kits and drivers. One builder on Instructables, for example, used Focal drivers from the same product lines found in JM Lab's Grande Utopia, a speaker that once sold for $40,000, to build a DIY version for around $3,000. That's less than one-tenth of the cost, though matching a flagship's sound depends heavily on the builder's skill. Leading DIY audio retailers like Parts Express, GR-Research, Madisound, and DIY Sound Group offer expertly matched driver and crossover kits made for bookshelf, tower, and subwoofer projects. Custom speaker cabinet building is certainly rewarding for the right kind of builder, with high-end projects being one of the best audio upgrades for home theater enthusiasts wanting uncompromised soundstage clarity. So how hard is it to build your own speakers? From an electronics standpoint, it's easier than building a PC, especially when using pre-matched component kits and pre-cut enclosures that handle all the complex acoustic mathematics. But understanding the core electromechanical components is going to make the process of building a custom DIY speaker easier to grasp. Every basic speaker is built with transducer drivers, such as woofers, midranges, and tweeters. Then there's the passive crossover circuit alongside an airtight cabinet enclosure to separate in-phase and out-of-phase sound waves. Component kits certainly save money on speaker hardware, but beginners need to consider the hidden startup costs of setting up a woodworking environment if they want to make their own enclosures. Building a custom enclosure is going to require proper woodworking tools like table saws and plunge routers with circle jigs. Then there are pipe clamps for gluing panels together, a soldering iron for the electronics, and some nice veneers for a professional finish. Enclosure material selection and airtight construction have to be right; otherwise, builders will introduce unwanted cabinet resonance and sound distortion. Dense, acoustically dead materials like medium-density fiberboard (MDF) or Medex combined with mitered joints and internal bracing are perfect for sturdy, non-resonant speaker boxes. There are a few prerequisites to have in a builder's arsenal before diving into DIY speakers. Getting the most out of your speakers requires understanding audio setup guidelines, as no one needs to be in the middle of a project asking themselves, "What is the 83% rule for speaker placement?" In room acoustics and speaker setup, the 83% rule refers to maintaining proper proportional geometry, such as setting the distance between the left and right speakers to roughly 83% of the total distance from the speakers to the primary listening position to optimize stereo imaging. Then there's the passive crossover circuit, which acts as the traffic controller within a speaker, directing specific frequency bands to the correct drivers. Passive crossovers use capacitors, inductors, and resistors to create low-pass, high-pass, and bandpass filters that prevent low frequencies from damaging tweeters. This can all be a lot to understand at first glance, but it's just a case of planning and mapping out components beforehand and sticking to the build plan. Internal cabinet lining is also needed to absorb rear sound waves and prevent internal standing wave echoes from muddying the output. Lining the inside walls with self-adhesive acoustic foam, Black Hole 5, or dense polyester fill absorbs internal sound reflections without holding back driver cone displacement. Finally, ask yourself: "How many surround sound speakers does your living room actually need?" The answer will help builders decide on cabinet sizes, driver counts, and amplifier requirements. There's nothing worse than spending time on a DIY speaker setup only to find it's not fit for purpose.

Reset  Apple delivered a strong finish to its fiscal year with record September-quarter results that topped Wall Street estimates, yet shares tumbled as investors focused on a projected margin squeeze from soaring memory costs and a cooling services outlook under new CEO John Ternus. The company reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% from a year earlier and ahead of the roughly $113.4 billion consensus, with diluted earnings per share of $2.10 beating the $1.99 estimate (aided in part by tariff refunds). iPhone revenue hit a September-quarter record of $57.58 billion, up about 17%, even with a staggered launch that included only limited sales of the iPhone 18 Pro models. Services reached an all-time high near $31.6 billion, while Mac sales jumped roughly 24%. iPad and Wearables declined on tough comparisons and supply constraints. Full fiscal 2026 revenue reached a company record of about $479 billion. Shares, which closed Monday at $338.32, fell as much as roughly 4% in after-hours trading during the earnings call and were down about 4% in Tuesday premarket trading near $325, erasing more than $170 billion in market value from the company’s roughly $4.9 trillion valuation if the losses held. The sell-off was driven primarily by guidance rather than the beat. Apple projected December-quarter (holiday) revenue growth of 7% to 10% — ahead of expectations and what would be an all-time record period — but guided gross margin to 45%–46%, down from 47.9% in the September quarter and below the roughly 47% analysts anticipated. Services growth was forecast at 8%–9%, short of the roughly 10.7% expected. On his first earnings call as CEO, Ternus described the memory-pricing environment as “unprecedented,” noting higher costs versus the prior quarter and warning they would rise further into the December period as Apple’s cheaper inventory advantage fades amid competition for components from AI infrastructure demand. Margins also face pressure from the ramp of its AI-powered Siri features. Analysts noted the results were solid on the hardware side — particularly the resilient iPhone franchise that underpins the ecosystem — but flagged concerns that non-iPhone businesses are not fully pulling their weight, alongside elevated costs and a high valuation (near 35 times forward earnings). Some also pointed to a Greater China miss relative to certain forecasts and broader consumer cost-of-living pressures that could limit Apple’s ability to pass through higher component prices. The reaction underscores a classic post-earnings dynamic for high-multiple tech names: strong past results can be overshadowed by any sign of near-term profit compression, especially heading into a critical holiday season and amid persistent supply-chain and AI-related spending pressures. Apple continues to emphasize its installed base, pricing power, and product pipeline, including the recent iPhone Duo foldable and other launches, but investors appear focused on whether margin headwinds will prove temporary or more persistent.  ‎ MacDailyNews Take:  Everybody is dealing wth soaring memory costs and Apple customers are, by far, the best positioned to absorb price increases while Apple is, by far, the company that’s best positioned to absorb component price fluctuations thanks to margins that are the envy of the industry. Apple’s so called “competitors” have no such luxuries. They have only price-sensitive (read: cheap and/or poor) customers and little room to maneuver with low or no margins. Net result: As Apple customers keep buying while rivals’ customers balk, Apple gains market share in every market in which they participate. Patience, AAPL padawans. This too shall pass. As the AI era continues to find its footing in the consumer market, “Cyclon” is a new smartphone/software experience that, to start, is reusing old Google Pixel phones with a software experience that literally uses AI to do every little thing. And my biggest question is just…  who actually wants this? The pitch of Cyclon, the founders explain in a video on Twitter/X, is to “[build] an AI phone to replace the iPhone.” And the central experience seems to be… talking to a chatbot. Examples in the video include telling the AI to “handle my notifications” and letting it monitor a WhatsApp message and reply to a friend asking for photos by grabbing those photos from your gallery without you as the user needing to touch the device.  Other examples on the company’s website have mixed utility at a glance. “Order my usual on DoorDash” and calling a courier to let them into a building certainly could be useful, but “tell the group chat I’m running ten minutes late” only to have the AI send the message on WhatsApp “in your words” not only seems like a waste of time, but a pointless disconnect from reality (as is all too common with these AI ventures). The one thing that caught my attention here is building apps on demand and being able to share them. The example given is a language learning app tailored to a specific vacation. It’s a really cool idea, though one I would imagine will have some rocky edges. Google is on a similar track with Gemini Intelligence’s “Create my widget” feature (on that note, when is that releasing on phones Google?), and I’d imagine Gemini will be able to do the same thing in time. The actual hardware side of things is also… interesting. Cyclon says that it has a working prototype of the idea running on Google Pixel 8a units, and it’ll ship “first-batch” backers one of those units with their $199 pre-order of a later “Cyclon Phone” that itself is expected to cost $699 – so you’re getting two phones for $699. That alone seems a little questionable in the midst of RAMageddon, but I digress.  That “final” phone hardware… sure is something. There are some good ideas here, some big promises, but more than anything I just want to know who actually wants to use a phone like this. I’m all for the idea of AI making my life a little easier (despite finding hardly any ways it can do that so far), but sending everything through a chatbot that does everything in the background and even generates “your words” for responses to my friends and family just sounds awful. And the state of social media isn’t exactly helping matters here. Twitter/X is 90% AI replies for engagement for this sort of thing, and Cyclon is paying influencers to boost that engagement too, so genuine reactions just seem impossible to find.  Sound off in the comments below if you’re an actual human with an opinion on this one, because I’m dying to know what real people think of this. Razer has teamed up with Neon Genesis Evangelion to introduce a new collection of gaming peripherals inspired by EVA-01, the iconic purple-and-green Evangelion unit piloted by Shinji Ikari. The Razer EVANGELION (EVA-01) Collection brings the anime’s distinctive visual identity to five pieces of gaming hardware and furniture, letting fans create a coordinated desktop setup. Following the earlier EVA-02 collaboration, the new collection focuses on EVA-01’s recognizable purple armor, neon-green accents, and mechanical detailing. Instead of limiting the collaboration to a mouse and keyboard, Razer has extended the theme across desktop audio, accessories, and seating, making it a more comprehensive gaming setup. Designer: Razer        Leading the collection is the Razer DeathAdder V4 Pro – EVANGELION (EVA-01) Edition. Based on Razer’s lightweight wireless gaming mouse, it features an ergonomic design and HyperSpeed Wireless Gen-2 connectivity for responsive control. The most distinctive addition, however, is an exclusive EVA-01 display stand. Inspired by the docking platform used to secure the Evangelion unit before deployment, the assembled stand provides a dedicated resting place for the mouse while doubling as a display piece. The Razer BlackWidow V4 TKL HyperSpeed – EVANGELION (EVA-01) Edition deploys the same visual treatment to a tenkeyless mechanical keyboard. Its compact layout leaves more room for mouse movement, while hot-swappable switches allow users to customize the typing experience without soldering. Wireless connectivity and low-latency performance retain the functionality expected from a gaming-focused keyboard.        For desktop audio, Razer has included the Leviathan V2 X – EVANGELION (EVA-01) Edition. The compact USB-C-powered soundbar is designed to sit beneath a monitor, keeping the desk relatively uncluttered. The EVA-01-inspired finish is complemented by Razer Chroma RGB lighting, extending the collection’s visual identity beyond conventional gaming peripherals. Completing the desktop accessories is the Gigantus V2 XXL – EVANGELION (EVA-01) Edition. Its expansive surface provides room for broad mouse movements, while the textured cloth material is designed to support consistent tracking. The largest piece of furniture in the lineup is the Iskur V2 X – EVANGELION (EVA-01) Edition gaming chair, which combines the collection’s purple-and-green styling with integrated lumbar support for extended gaming sessions.   The collection for now is an Asia-Pacific exclusive, with pre-orders expected through Amazon and selected regional retail partners. Availability may vary by market, though. Reported Japanese retail prices are ¥32,980 (approximately $215) for the mouse, ¥35,980 ($235) for the keyboard, ¥22,980 ($150) for the soundbar, ¥6,980 ($45) for the mouse mat, and ¥69,980 ($455) for the chair. With five coordinated products, Razer’s latest collaboration goes beyond applying an anime-inspired colour scheme to existing hardware. The exclusive mouse stand adds a collectible element, while the remaining products make it possible to carry the EVA-01 aesthetic across your entire dedicated gaming workspace. We may be long past the days of requiring extraordinarily ugly impact bumpers be affixed to cars sold in the U.S., with those laws extending to supercars like the Lamborghini Countach, cars that are driving around on American roads still aren't quite as smooth as they may be in other markets. Whether for insurance reasons like the Bugatti Chiron or to meet regulatory crash safety regulations, U.S.-spec versions of some cars (typically wild-looking, high-end ones) sometimes get bumpers that protrude slightly further out, or have bumperettes or bumper guards added on. The latest victim of this is the Jaguar Type 01, except its little U.S.-spec bumperette solution is actually extremely well done, perfectly integrated with its outrageous styling. I got to see the Type 01 in person for the first time at the Las Vegas Concours over the weekend, and I love it even more in the metal than I already did in photos. Luckily our American-market modifications haven't ruined that. At the bottom of the body-color strakes in the upright rear end, the Type 01 has a black bar stretching across the same width that houses the parking sensors, with the license plate holder sitting just below it along with a fang-like diffuser design. On the U.S.-spec Type 01, that black bar juts outward a little more dramatically, with angled sections at the ends instead of it being flat all the way across. The rest of the rear end design is exactly the same, and the protruding bumper flows so perfectly with the car's design, you probably wouldn't even notice it if the two cars were side by side. There is one other difference between Euro- and U.S.-spec Type 01s you may have noticed. Here in America our cars need to have side marker lights and reflectors at front and the rear; usually automakers will integrated these as subtly as possible, maybe along the curve of the wheel arches, following the design of the bumper, or even putting them within the headlights and taillights themselves. Jaguar, though, decided to make them a more prominent part of the car's design. The Type 01's side markers are squares, positioned low down in the corners of the front and rear bumpers where their lines are aligned with other lines of the car. Yeah, they stand out, and some people will find them to be an eyesore, but I actually like this placement. At least nothing else about the Type 01's lighting design had to be changed for the U.S. market — the headlight arrays are still ultra-thin, and the pair of full-width taillights are still hidden between those strakes. Other than those two little details, the Type 01's design is identical across markets, which is a good thing. Love it or hate it, you've got to respect Jaguar really swinging for the fences here and creating production car with pure concept-y looks, like it traveled back in time to show off how wild cars will look in the future.

Adding another B2B marketing channel only helps if your team can capture the interest it creates and evaluate whether that investment is working. A promising traffic report is not the same as evidence that a campaign generated additional demand. In How To Create Demand You Can Actually Convert (And Prove), Shaun Bruno, Senior Growth Marketing Manager at CallRail, and Colin Saunders of Matter Made explained how they approached channel selection, secured funding for tests, and measured results before scaling spend. Bruno described how CallRail simplified its marketing mix around paid search and the landing pages needed to convert existing demand. The team then strengthened measurement, clarified its ideal customer profile, and built out consideration and retargeting programs before investing further in awareness. That sequence mattered more than copying CallRail’s full channel mix. As Shaun Bruno put it: “But the important takeaway is that you don’t need to run all these channels.” See the full on-demand clip at 11:40. His broader point was that the bottom of the funnel needed to support the demand created at the top. More reach would not repair a landing page, offer, or follow-up process that failed to convert interested buyers. Saunders distinguished between the buying patterns his agency encountered among smaller businesses and enterprise accounts. For SMB and mid-market programs with existing search demand, paid search offered a way to reach people actively researching a solution and establish acquisition benchmarks. Enterprise programs often needed more education and time to engage a buying group, so his team leaned more heavily on paid social. He presented these as starting approaches, not a universal channel split for every business. The channel decision also depended on what the buyer would encounter after the click. Saunders connected positioning, the offer, and creative: a demo request, an educational resource, and a product video served different needs. He described testing creative and landing-page content against the audience’s stage rather than expecting one asset to do every job. The presenters emphasized defining a test’s business purpose before pitching a new platform. Saunders outlined three requirements: identify the problem, agree on the measurement and reporting cadence, and set a timeframe with a decision date. For a lean budget, he recommended narrowing the audience or geography instead of spreading spend across a national market. A smaller test could investigate a specific segment, provided leadership understood what it could reveal and how long it needed to run. He also stressed connecting advertising data with CRM outcomes. Form submissions could provide an early signal, but the team needed visibility into whether those leads became opportunities and customers. That distinction helped turn a request for more traffic into a business case for further investment. Bruno described using the comparison to support a broader rollout, then monitoring acquisition efficiency as spend increased. The useful lesson was the progression: early signals justified a more rigorous experiment, and that experiment informed the next investment decision. The pilot was a case study, not a guarantee that another advertiser would see the same result. A rise in branded search could strengthen the case for further investigation; it was not interchangeable with a directly attributed conversion or proof of incremental revenue. The presenters also discussed self-reported attribution as another source of context, rather than treating any one measurement as the whole story. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Retired filmmaker John Carpenter is best known for his horror films. After all, we don't have the modern slasher film without "Halloween." But before Michael Myers returned to Haddonfield on Halloween night 1978, Carpenter tried his hand at an action-exploitation film: 1976's "Assault on Precinct 13," which opened in theaters 50 years ago today. Carpenter was born in 1948, the perfect age to grow up on cowboy movies. He dreamed of going to Hollywood to make Westerns, not horror films. But, by the time he enrolled in University of South California film school in 1968, Westerns had already faded as Hollywood's biggest genre. Throughout his decades-long filmmaking career, Carpenter never directed a Western — but you can see that longing in "Assault on Precinct 13." The movie has a courageous lawman who has to hold his ground against the black hat gangs. The catch? The movie is set in contemporary Los Angeles, not the Wild West. Lieutenant Ethan Bishop (Austin Stoker) is overseeing the closure of the LAPD's Precinct 13. A prison bus, carrying convicted murderer Napoleon Wilson (Darwin Joston), also stops at the precinct for a respite. Before long, the building is under siege by bloodthirsty gang members. Bishop, Wilson, and surviving secretary Leigh (Laurie Zimmer) are in a literal fight for their lives as unlikely allies. Made on a meager budget of $100,000, "Assault on Precinct 13" wasn't an instant mega-hit. Reviews weren't too enthusiastic either. Whitney Williams of Variety was ambivalent, writing backhanded praise like, "some exciting action in second half packs enough interest to keep this entry alive for the violence market." Ellen Edwards of The Miami Herald condemned the film for its "hideous, unmotivated violence." But "Assault on Precinct 13" found its audience. It even got a remake in 2005, starring Laurence Fishburne and Ethan Hawke. One of John Carpenter's acknowledged influences for "Assault on Precinct 13" is one of the most beloved Westerns ever: Howard Hawks' "Rio Bravo," about a sheriff (John Wayne) and his deputies trying to keep a murderer with a rich brother and many hired guns locked up. But "Rio Bravo" is not a tense thriller; often called a hangout movie, it's leisurely paced with only bursts of gun violence.  In "Assault on Precinct 13," the threat is everywhere. There's not even a reason for the siege beyond violence for its own sake; there's nothing of value inside the precinct besides more lives to end. That leads into one of the other movies that inspired Carpenter: George Romero's 1968 "Night of the Living Dead," the first modern zombie movie. When asked if "Night of the Living Dead" inspired "Assault on Precinct 13," Carpenter said, half-seriously, "Everybody who made a low-budget film was inspired by ['Night of the Living Dead']." The comparison rings even more true here. Both movies are about people trapped inside a small building, surrounded by a horde outside that wants to break in and kill them. Both films also cast a Black man as their hero: Stoker as Lt. Bishop in "Precinct 13" and Duane Jones as Ben in "Night of the Living Dead." That was a bigger deal in the 1960s and '70s than it is now, and one spot where Carpenter's exploitation movie is rather progressive. "Living Dead" ends on a famously cynical note, with Ben shot by white men who mistook him as a threat. In "Precinct 13," Bishop and Napoleon Wilson achieve mutual respect; at the end of the movie, they walk out of the basement together as equals. After its U.S. theatrical release in 1976, "Assault on Precinct 13" played along the European festival circuit, including the Cannes Film Festival and the London Film Festival. (At the latter, it received "deafening applause" per a contemporary review by The Guardian's Derek Malcolm.) Seeing the movie at Cannes, George Romero paid forward the compliment of Carpenter modeling his movie after "Night of the Living Dead." The most shocking scene in "Assault on Precinct 13" is when a little girl, Kathy (future reality TV star Kim Richards), is shot in the chest after buying an ice cream cone. It's a jaw-dropping scene, and the movie is clearly having perverse fun turning such a taboo of violence against children into a spectacle and sick joke.  Quoted in Jason Zinoman's "Shock Value: How a Few Eccentric Outsiders Gave Us Nightmares, Conquered Hollywood, and Invented Modern Horror," Romero testified to this scene's impact: "John Carpenter at Cannes wiped us off the face of the earth with 'Precinct 13.' Right from the scene when the little girl gets blown away, I was blown away." (The same book reports that, to get an R instead of an X rating, Carpenter cut the girl's death from the rating review board then added it back in before the film went to theaters.) This sort of gang violence is echoed in Carpenter's later "Escape From New York," which is all about a future where the gangs like those in "Precinct 13" have taken over the Big Apple. Like "Escape from New York" and many of his other movies, Carpenter also composed the score for "Precinct 13." The title sequence theme, a synthesized anthem of droning dread, is still the most perfect mood setter for an action thriller even 50 years later.

The product category search responds to parent categories again, and the documentation got some improvements. For an in depth overview of the Tryton issues please take a look at our issue tracker or see the issues and merge requests filtered by label. When you search for a product category by name, the parent categories are matched as well. The stock documentation now describes the procedure for setting lots on assigned moves. The sale credit limit module documentation has been refreshed to match the latest behaviour and configuration options. The move grouping wizard now has its own section in the accounting documentation. We released bug fixes for the recently released 8.2 minor series and the currently maintained long term support series 8.0, 7.8, and 7.0. The product category now extends the tree() domain instead of overriding it. Overriding could mask the contribution of the tree() mixin to search_rec_name, so anyone who reuses the search override pattern should leave the tree() clause extension in place. The party replacement now takes an optional WHERE clause to restrict the rows that are updated. The clause is provided by a hook on the model, so developers can keep certain rows (such as moves that have already been voided) untouched while the rest of the party field is rewritten. SpaceX joined several other issuers objecting to OKXICE tokenized trading, months after crypto platforms offered tokens tied to its shares. Just months after tokenized versions of SpaceX shares became one of the biggest drivers of  onchain stock trading, the aerospace company is pushing back against plans to bring similar trading to US investors. According to a Nov. 2 public notice from OKXICE, SpaceX has objected to the proposed listing of tokenized versions of its shares on the trading venue, a joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE). The company now joins Tesla and Amazon among 56 companies objecting to the proposed listings. Under the Securities and Exchange Commission’s five-year Innovation Exemption introduced in September, platforms such as OKXICE can offer trading in tokenized versions of US stocks without registering as national securities exchanges. But the framework also gives companies a say in the process: They have 30 days to object to the proposed trading of their shares tokenized by third parties, effectively keeping those tokens off the venue. Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based representations of company shares that allow investors to gain exposure to traditional equities onchain, often around the clock. Depending on the structure, they can be backed by actual shares, although the rights granted to tokenholders may differ from those of traditional shareholders. OKXICE co-chair and former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo told Cointelegraph on Oct. 20 that the venture expected more objections as companies avoided being the first to test the model.  SpaceX’s objection comes despite tokenized versions of its shares already trading on platforms outside the US, where they have attracted significant trading activity since the company’s June public offering. Ahead of the SpaceX listing, Backpack Securities, a stock brokerage and tokenization platform, and crypto exchange Kraken, through its xStocks offering, both prepared tokenized versions of the aerospace company’s stock, each designed to be backed by actual shares. Backpack’s SPCX token went on to record $1.08 billion in onchain trading volume in June, while Kraken’s SPCXx token recorded $852 million. Unlike Backpack and Kraken, OKXICE would open tokenized stock trading to US investors under the SEC’s new regulatory framework, potentially tapping into the world’s largest equity market by capitalization and expanding the investor base for tokenized securities. Nasdaq warned issuers in September that they “must be cautious about their participation” in the venture, arguing that tokenized stock trading could fragment liquidity and undermine long-term shareholder value. Despite the growing opposition, Cuomo said during an Oct. 30 press conference that as people see the benefits of tokenization, “you’ll see more and more companies participate.”  Cointelegraph is committed to providing independent, high-quality journalism across the crypto, blockchain, AI, and fintech industries.
