By Anthony Franco |   at November 2, 2026 10:50pm CDT   Rangers center fielder Evan Carter underwent labrum surgery on his right hip last week, president of baseball operations Chris Young told reporters on Monday (link via Kennedi Landry of MLB.com). Young said that while Carter is expected to play for a good portion of the 2027 season, he’s not likely to be ready for Opening Day — presuming the season itself starts on time. It’s yet another injury setback for Carter, who battled back issues early in his career. He had a relatively healthy ’26 campaign in terms of avoiding the injured list, only missing two weeks in the middle of June with a right oblique strain. Carter easily established new career highs in games played (141) and plate appearances (455) but slogged through a miserable offensive season. He batted .194/.288/.315 with nine home runs. Among hitters with 400+ PAs, only Cal Raleigh and Matt McLain had a lower batting average. Carter was fifth from the bottom in slugging and in the bottom 15 in on-base percentage despite a strong 10.3% walk rate. He struck out a quarter of the time and made a lot of weak contact. Carter also continued to struggle mightily in limited looks against left-handed pitching; he’s a .110 hitter and still doesn’t have an extra-base hit against a southpaw in his major league career (145 plate appearances). The Rangers should’ve been in the center field market even if Carter were fully healthy. His injury only makes that a more urgent need. Young acknowledged as much, at least in the immediate future. “It doesn’t change our belief in Evan long term, but it does change our short-term plans that we need to have a backfill (with) somebody who can certainly fill in or play a very solid center field and hopefully contribute offensively,” he told reporters. The alternative would be to play Wyatt Langford up the middle. Langford is an above-average runner who has posted plus defensive grades in his 523 1/3 career innings as a center fielder. He’s among the game’s best defensive left fielders and was a Gold Glove finalist in the corner this year. Langford should be capable of playing a quality center field, though the Rangers would still need to add a corner outfielder opposite Brandon Nimmo. They’re otherwise looking at the likes of Alejandro Osuna and Cam Cauley playing regular roles. That’s before considering the idea that even a healthy Carter might not be a long-term answer. Although Young stressed publicly that they’re still bullish on the 24-year-old’s future, he’s a career .215/.307/.368 hitter who at least needs a right-handed hitting platoon partner. Texas could continue giving top shortstop prospect Sebastian Walcott reps in the outfield, but there’s also the possibility that they try to line up a Corey Seager trade this winter. Luis Robert Jr., Daulton Varsho, Trent Grisham, Tyrone Taylor, Cedric Mullins and Myles Straw are options in a weak free agent center field class. Robert and Taylor are righty bats who could shield Carter from southpaws when he’s healthy. Grisham is probably better suited for a corner spot at this stage of his career (though Texas could sign him to play left and use Langford in center). Taylor Ward is available as another left field option. The trade market could feature the likes of Steven Kwan, Jake McCarthy, Jarren Duran, Colton Cowser and Dane Myers. Texas also has needs at catcher, designated hitter/first base, and potentially second base depending on their plan for Walcott. Hello Jarren Duran! This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. India’s economy and its stock market are not seeing eye to eye. As the nation begins its busiest part of the year marked by a string of festivals and harvests, consumer demand is skyrocketing. Firms selling everything from shampoos to jewellery are reporting robust demand—and even managing to raise prices. Yet the stocks of bellwethers like Hindustan Unilever and Maruti Suzuki have sunk to multi-year lows.  Indian stocks have underperformed global markets for more than two years, losing nearly half their value, as foreign capital fled. Disappointing earnings, scant exposure to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, and external shocks such as US tariffs and oil-price spikes from the Iran war have all weighed on returns.  As global money managers ran out of reasons to invest, some bulls nursed one hope—that once consumer demand accelerated, corporate earnings would improve, offsetting the drag and reviving returns.  Now, even that flicker is being doused. The latest quarterly results show that a consumption boom is unlikely to end stocks’ underperformance. We may well be heading into a paradoxical period—rapid economic growth co-existing with an equity market in the doldrums. Consumer demand among the country’s 1.5 billion people is coming back with a roar. The e-commerce market is heading for its fastest growth in five years and will hit a record $90 billion in 2026, as per Redseer Strategy Consultants. The trend growth in consumer demand has moved up a couple of notches, according to official data. Businesses are reporting double-digit sales growth. Most are hiking prices because of robust demand. But that’s not enough for investors. They now value resilience more than headline growth. Shareholders have little appetite for consumer firms pursuing growth by surrendering profit margins. Shares are being valued for the minimum rate of expansion the country can sustain in the wake of external pressures, especially surging oil prices.  The economy is particularly vulnerable to oil prices. India imports almost 90% of its crude-oil needs. That’s starting to hurt profitability. Eight months into the Iran war, the average profit of firms in the Sensex is coming in 11% below forecasts made a year ago.   Higher fuel and freight costs also are feeding into food prices and other everyday goods, and will eventually curtail how much households spend. It’s that future possibility stocks are pricing in.  The inflation imported through higher oil prices will persist until the Iran war ends and economists expect it to remain high well into 2027. Investors evaluating the financial results of consumer companies are already finding some of that stress seeping through. Escalating commodity prices are lifting costs even as demand is outstripping supply. Crude-derived ingredients and other input prices are making it expensive to produce everything from soaps to cosmetics, and price hikes are not enough to offset that.  The calendar is choc-a-bloc with festivals from October to January, when families spend on ritual-linked purchases that are considered necessities rather than discretionary. That’s giving a short-term boost to corporate profits, but would dry up when the season is over. So what can end India’s equity-market underperformance? In the short term, the Iran war needs to end before a durable bull can return. The unwinding of the AI frenzy could also help, given that India is increasingly seen as a market that benefits from a rotation away from the technology boom.   The government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) also have parts to play. Containing inflation and stabilizing the rupee will be essential to restoring investor confidence. But an interest-rate hike by RBI, on its own, is unlikely to deliver either outcome.  New Delhi must closely monitor supplies of grains and vegetables across the country, and prevent shortages fuelled by hoarding and speculation. State governments, meanwhile, should consider switching to fixed per-litre fuel levies rather than percentage-based taxes, which automatically generate higher revenues as oil prices rise. The latter creates an incentive for local authorities to benefit from precisely the price increases that are hurting consumers. Over the longer term, India must reduce its dependence on fossil fuels. It needs a transition towards renewable energy and alternative sources of power if it’s to break the recurring cycle of oil shocks, pressure on the rupee, depletion of foreign-exchange reserves, and the need for the central bank to resort to increasingly restrictive currency-management measures. For now, India’s consumers and its stock market are telling very different stories.  If the spending boom is to endure, a strong economy on its own is not enough to convince investors that it’s time to pile back in. ©Bloomberg The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist. In September, Bitget, one of the world's larger crypto exchanges, lost about $352 million from its internet-connected wallets. A year and a half earlier, Bybit lost about $1.5 billion. Indian investors remember WazirX, which lost about $230 million in July 2024 and froze withdrawals for months. Over the same period, US spot Bitcoin ETFs have grown to hold more than $100 billion of Bitcoin. None of them has reported losing any to a hack. Both groups hold the same asset, on the same network. So why do exchanges keep losing customers' Bitcoin while ETFs do not? The answer has little to do with Bitcoin itself, and a lot to do with what each institution is built to do. An exchange exists to exchange. Its customers expect to buy, sell and withdraw at 3am on a Sunday, so a meaningful part of its holdings has to sit in "hot" wallets, connected to the internet and able to sign transactions in seconds. Every connection, every employee with signing rights and every software vendor adds to what security teams call the attack surface. Bybit's loss is instructive: the funds were taken while being moved from cold storage to a warm wallet, through a compromised signing interface. The weak point was not the vault. It was the door, and an exchange opens that door many times a day. An ETF exists to hold. It has a daily cut-off, much like the stock market it trades on. New money is collected through the day and settled in a single batch. That rhythm means the Bitcoin can stay offline, in cold storage, with the signing keys split across locations and several independent people required to approve any movement. The custodian is usually a specialist appointed to do exactly one thing: keep the asset safe. It does not trade, lend or chase volume. The distinction is between access and safekeeping. An exchange must optimise for access, and it pays for that in risk. A custodian can optimise for safekeeping, and pays for it in convenience: moving assets takes hours, not seconds. This is not to say ETFs carry no risk. A large share of US ETF Bitcoin sits with a small number of custodians, which concentrates operational risk, and Bitcoin's price remains volatile whichever way it is held. But the specific risk that has cost exchange customers billions, a breach of internet-connected wallets, is largely designed out of the custodial model. The same principle is available to Indian investors who do not buy ETFs abroad. Platforms like BitSave that keep 100% of client assets with an institutional custodian in cold storage, and publish verifiable proof of reserves that anyone can verify 24x7 on the blockchain, follow the ETF model rather than the exchange model. The question for a long-term investor, then, is not only what to buy, but where it will sit. If the plan is to hold for a decade, an asset does not need to be one click from a sale. It needs to be hard to steal. Since launching in 2025, the Kia PV5 has brought some big, new energy to the camper van scenes in debut markets like South Korea and Europe. And we're not talking solely about its all-electric energy, but about the fact that it's becoming something of a modern day Volkswagen T1 in offering a fun-sized base van representing boundless road-trip freedom. Now, another continent gets to experience that same energy, as KombiLife brings to market what it hails as "Australia's first PV5 camper:" the Kia Weekender.  While most of the world's population prepares for an El Niño-powered winter, Australians are just hitting their late-spring stride on the way to summer. And KombiLife's Weekender package arrives just in time to become the ideal little camper van for all types of multi-day road trip, light cross-continent overlanding and holiday camping.  Like any good Australian camper van, the Kia Weekender has been built up to tackle the rough, unsealed roads that are unavoidable in the Outback and other parts of the country. Given that Kia doesn't so much as offer all-wheel drive on its tiny modular electric van (the larger PV7 will get AWD), we wouldn't exactly call it an all-out off-road adventure machine, but KombiLife does toughen it up with a set of knobby Falken Wildpeak 215/65R16 all-terrain tires and a model-specific bull bar topped by Stedi auxiliary pod lights up front.  It's no Epicore Action Van, but it's the first Kia PV5 we've covered with an off-road package of this sort. It might not hold its place as ruggedest Kia PV5 camper van for long as more and more businesses ride the PV5's popularity to exciting new camper designs, but it's definitely earned the rank for now.  Beyond the modestly burlified exterior, KombiLife really digs in on its work inside the cabin, combining elements from a number of PV5 campers and other small camper van packages to create what looks like a comfortable, high-functioning base camp.  We haven't yet covered a PV5 camper with the classic mini-camper layout that pairs a long sofa running along one sidewall with a kitchen or storage unit across the way, so the Weekender becomes the first. Because the launch model lacks a pop-up roof for standing up, KombiLife pushes the kitchen outside for better ergonomics and dedicates the passenger side to a tall storage console with slim shelf on top and storage cubbies below. The sofa is a simple design meant to seat both occupants comfortably before expanding out into a 75 x 47-in (190 x 120-cm) double bed.  Beyond creating a cozy day/night space out of the PV5's compact interior, the split-sided conversion also leaves a clear center aisle for travel. KombiLife encourages owners to fill that space out with the likes of a bicycle, surfboards, skis or other adventure sports gear requiring a lengthy storage berth. The outdoor kitchen brings the design more in line with PV5 campers like the Dutch-designed Vantrack Lightcamp. This opens up the standing space you'll want when cooking while inviting you to enjoy the fresh air and scenic outdoor spaces you traveled to see. The kitchen slide-out features a Dometic twin-hob induction cooktop beside a worktop, along with storage cabinets large enough for pots and pans down below. The unit slides away below the sofa after use.  In place of an inbuilt sink, the Weekender kitchen uses more of deconstructed design with 11-L Dometic canister and Go faucet supplying a collapsible basin on the opposite side of the van from the slide-out. We'd prefer to see this system on a slide-out of its own, just so accidental spills end up on the ground and not the camper floor, but it is an efficient design that saves space to keep the camper small and light without giving up any critical cooking and cleaning capabilities.  Once the meal has been prepared, Weekender campers can enjoy it on the swivel table mounted up near the front of the sofa. They can sit in the swivel driver's cab seats or on the sofa, where it'll be easy to grab a drink from the 30-L fridge located in a drawer under the front of the sofa.  Instead of adding the complexity and expense of a separate leisure battery and electrical system, KombiLifie relies on the vehicle-to-load capability of the PV5's 71-kWh traction battery. It says it delivers ample power to run the induction cooktop and even additional appliances like a microwave or toaster. The shop does wire in an electrical subsystem to lower the voltage for equipment running on 12-V DC power, including the fridge, lights and fans.  "The PV5 has everything you want in a conversion base: a flat floor, generous space, a real 416 km (258 miles) of range, and a price that's within reach," raves KombiLife Director Mark Kofahl. "And because the van itself is the battery, we've been able to leave out the auxiliary battery system entirely."  One feature of the PV5 that promises to be quite a boon for campers traveling through the extreme temperatures of Australia is the van's "Utility Mode," which allows campers to run the vehicular climate control system through the night without further draining the battery by keeping other vehicle systems running. So in addition to integrated electrical power, campers enjoy integrated heating and air conditioning.  KombiLife finishes off its interior handiwork with some strategically placed organization. Commentary             Commentary     Retail investors should be cautious about buying or selling shares simply because they read in the news that an analyst has changed a recommendation, says NTU finance professor Roger Loh.         This audio is generated by an AI tool.      SINGAPORE: Shares of at least two Singapore-listed firms made headlines last month after their shares fell sharply following downgrades by stock market analysts. OCBC shares tumbled nearly 6 per cent on Oct 7 after Citi cited softer-than-expected third-quarter earnings expectations and downgraded the bank to “sell”. Days later, Sheng Siong shares fell as much as 3 per cent on the back of a downgrade by Maybank to “hold” and a cut in target price. How can a single analyst’s opinion have such a dramatic impact on a company’s share price? Should retail investors follow these recommendations? Analysts employed by financial institutions study the companies they cover, forecast their earnings and recommend whether investors should buy, hold, or sell their shares. Their research helps institutional investors assess what companies are worth, with the information ultimately reflected in market prices. A vibrant analyst research sector is therefore an important part of a well-developed equity market. Thousands of investment professionals are constantly evaluating publicly-listed companies. For an analyst report to move a stock price significantly, it must offer new insights that investors have not yet incorporated into their valuations. In a 2011 study where my co-author and I examined more than 150,000 analyst recommendation changes for US stocks, we found only about one in eight such changes were accompanied by a large stock-price movement in the direction of the change. Most had no discernible impact on share prices, when measured from the day the recommendation was issued through the following trading day. To illustrate just how difficult it is to produce market-moving research, one in four analysts in our study never issued a single influential recommendation change. Even among those who had managed to move stock prices at least once, only one in five of their recommendation changes were significant. So, when does an analyst recommendation change become impactful? Track record matters. Analysts who have moved markets before, won awards or have a history of issuing recommendations ahead of their peers tend to be more influential. Recommendations that move away from the prevailing consensus, or are accompanied by earnings forecasts, are more likely to move stock prices too. Company characteristics also play a role. Analyst recommendations tend to be more influential for smaller companies, growth stocks, and companies where analysts disagree considerably about future earnings. These findings are based on historical US data but the underlying economic reasoning suggests that similar forces may operate here in the Singapore market.  Both the OCBC and Sheng Siong downgrades were accompanied by downward revisions to earnings forecasts. Citi's downgrade of OCBC was also clearly contrarian, going against the prevailing more positive views of other analysts. For retail investors, the crucial question is whether they can profit by following analyst recommendations they read about in the news. The answer is that it is difficult. Stock prices react very quickly to influential recommendations. Our research finds that almost all of the stock-price reaction around recommendations occurs on the day the report is issued and the following trading day.  By the time retail investors read about a downgrade in the news, much of the price adjustment may already have occurred. Academic studies have nevertheless found that share prices can continue moving in the direction of analyst recommendation changes for up to a month. Take the example of an investor who sold shares immediately after reading about the recent downgrades. They might have avoided further losses, but profiting from a single recommendation does not show that following analyst calls is a reliably profitable strategy. To reliably capture profits, investors have to react to analyst recommendations quickly – typically within a day – and trade systematically across many recommendation changes rather than just a few selected ones.  That is extremely difficult for retail investors who may only learn about these changes after prices have reacted. They are therefore unlikely to replicate these returns, particularly after accounting for trading costs such as brokerage commissions. This is why retail investors should be cautious about buying or selling shares simply because they read in the news that an analyst has changed a recommendation. This does not mean analyst reports are unimportant to retail investors. Their greatest value lies in helping investors understand companies rather than providing immediate trading signals. Instead of focusing solely on an analyst’s recommendation or target price, investors should examine the assumptions behind the recommendation. What earnings growth does the analyst expect? What are the key drivers of profitability? What risks could cause the forecast to be wrong? A downgrade does not necessarily mean a company's business has deteriorated. An analyst might still expect earnings to grow but conclude that the share price has risen too far relative to those prospects. Different analysts can also arrive at different recommendations because they make different assumptions about future earnings, risks and appropriate valuations. Rather than seeing these disagreements as confusing, investors should use them to identify the uncertainties that matter most. Access to analyst research also highlights the information gap between institutional and retail investors. This is not unique to Singapore. Full analyst reports are often available only to institutional clients or customers of the bank or brokerage producing the research. Retail investors without such access typically learn about recommendation changes in the news, often after much of the stock-price reaction has occurred. Moreover, media reports rarely contain the detailed analysis underlying these recommendations. In the past, retail investors might have lacked the time or expertise to digest lengthy analyst reports filled with technical jargon. Now, large language models can make it much easier for investors to understand these reports, compare analysts' assumptions, and identify key areas of disagreement. This makes access to the underlying research more valuable than ever. Initiatives such as the Grant for Equity Market Singapore (GEMS) programme, which supports research coverage of companies listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), are therefore welcome. SGX also posts a selection of analyst reports on its website. Greater efforts by exchanges and brokerages to make more analyst research accessible would help narrow the information gap between institutional and retail investors. Roger Loh is an Associate Professor and Deputy Head of the Division of Finance at Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University. Home > Law and Politics >                          When Funimation shut down in 2024, buyers of DVDs and Blu-ray discs that came with a Funimation digital release lost access to those copies. A fresh petition to the U.S. Copyright Office cites this as a reason for a DMCA exemption that would allow disc owners to make replacement copies for personal use. Rightsholders and other opponents of the proposal have until February to file their objections.               In April 2024, anime streaming service Funimation shut down its app and website, as it became part of Crunchyroll. The closure also cut off access to the Funimation digital copies that came with DVDs and Blu-ray discs. This wasn’t well received by anime fans. Today, Crunchyroll’s help page still states that it does not currently support these copies. Instead, the page encourages affected users to explore the anime streaming library that Crunchyroll does offer. Funimation digital copies     The movies and shows are still on the discs and in theory American buyers could make their own digital replacement copies. However, doing so would break the law as the DMCA’s anti-circumvention provision prohibits bypassing the encryption on DVDs and Blu-rays, unless an exemption applies. The U.S. Copyright Office reviews these exemptions every three years, and last week it opened ten proposed classes for public comment. Two of the underlying petitions deal with works for which digital access was discontinued, and one specifically mentions the Funimation case. One of these petitions comes from Jayden Milne. He asks the Office to allow owners of DVDs, Blu-ray and Ultra HD Blu-ray discs to make a single secured, local copy for personal use, when the digital copy promised on the packaging is no longer available.  That covers two situations. The first are people who redeemed a digital copy before the service behind it shut down, as happened with Funimation. The second are buyers of new discs whose code had already expired. According to the petition, Warner Bros. states that its digital codes expire based on a title’s release date rather than the purchase date, and that expired codes are not replaced. This means that a disc bought years after its release may come with a code that no longer works. Milne’s petition     Milne wants owners of these physical discs to be able to rip a replacement from them, under strict conditions. The replacement can’t be better than what was promised. If the box offered an HD digital copy, for example, owners can’t rip the 4K version. Also, the copy is for personal use and it must be destroyed if the disc is sold, given away or lost. A second and related petition, submitted by Zakaria Zerhouane, focuses on anime more broadly. It covers series and films that were removed from authorized U.S. streaming platforms after their licenses expired, as well as anime released on disc by U.S. distributors that no longer exist. The petition does not mention Funimation but lists several distributors, including ADV Films, Bandai Entertainment, Central Park Media and Geneon. In addition to bypassing encryption on discs, Zerhouane also wants to legally circumvent the DRM, geo-locking, and session-based access controls that streaming platforms use. This is needed, the petition argues, as the anime licensing market is unstable.  “Streaming platforms provide no advance removal notice, preventing users from finishing or preserving works before they disappear,” Zerhouane writes. Zerhouane’s petition     He adds that the consolidation of the U.S. anime market under “a single dominant entity” has made catalogs more volatile. The petition doesn’t name the company, but the description appears to fit Sony-owned Crunchyroll. Neither petition covers all video content. Zerhouane’s request is limited to anime, while Milne’s only covers discs that came with a digital copy. Both petitions are restricted to personal and noncommercial uses. The Copyright Office grouped these requests with four other ‘replacement’ petitions. These ask for personal backups of discs, including before they deteriorate, and permission to format-shift discs as playback hardware disappears. These become more relevant every year, as old formats decay. The Office notes that the Register of Copyrights has repeatedly declined to recommend such format-shifting exemptions in the past. This means that, while they are on the agenda, approval is uncertain. Before making any decision, the Office wants more details from stakeholders. It asks which copy protections are involved, whether the titles can be watched legally some other way, and why making these copies wouldn’t infringe copyright. It also wants to know whether allowing this would hurt sales. Supporters have until December 7 to send in their comments. Opponents can respond until February 22, and public hearings will follow in the spring. — A copy of the Copyright Office’s notice of proposed rulemaking is available here (pdf). Jayden Milne’s petition can be found here (pdf), and Zakaria Zerhouane’s petition is available here (pdf). Public cloud procurement needs a CMA roadmap to prevent lock-in  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  The CMA has published roadmaps for Big Tech before, just not for Microsoft. With £400 billion in annual public sector procurement and millions flowing to Microsoft’s cloud, the CMA can’t wait until February 2027 to act. The topic of public procurement is becoming a major issue for UK economic policy. Sarah Cardell, the CMA's Chief Executive, delivered a speech at a Parliamentary event at the House of Commons on 8 September, introducing two reports by the CMA published that day: Public Procurement in the National Interest and Rigged Bids, Real Costs. The headline conclusion is, perhaps unsurprisingly, that UK public procurement could be leveraged far more effectively to shape markets and improve outcomes for citizens, businesses and taxpayers alike. But a more nuanced point, and arguably the most important one, is that the biggest risks arise when short-term cost savings are prioritized at the expense of long-term value and competition. Director of Laganview Associates. Cloud computing is one of the starkest illustrations of this trade-off in practice. Buying Microsoft is, in the immediate term, the path of least resistance: it is already embedded in most public-sector IT estates, integration is straightforward, and the near-term cost of switching or diversifying looks far higher than the cost of simply renewing. That short-term logic is precisely why Microsoft has wound itself so tightly around the machinery of UK public-sector cloud infrastructure. Each individual procurement decision may look like sensible, low-risk value for money at the time it is taken but cumulatively, those decisions have entrenched a single supplier so deeply into public-sector data, identity and security architecture that it now poses a very real threat to competitive procurement in public-sector AI. The apparent saving today is a major liability for tomorrow, once every AI rollout has to be built on top of infrastructure only one vendor fully controls. The CMA's cloud market investigation reached a clear verdict in July 2025: competition wasn't working well. Microsoft and AWS each hold 30–40% market share with Microsoft's share still growing, and barriers to entry including data-center costs, economies of scale, incumbent product breadth. have been deemed likely to keep it that way. Apparently, fewer than 1 per cent of customers switch cloud providers annually, held back by egress fees and technical friction. Most tellingly, the CMA found Microsoft withholds certain licensed products from AWS and Google that directly weaken those rivals; a problem with clear implications for public-sector buyers seeking competitive procurement. However, as Microsoft rapidly rolls out new AI tools across UK enterprises and the public sector, the fundamental issue of cloud infrastructure lock-in is being overlooked. The true barrier to a competitive AI market isn't just the stickiness of new daily workflows, but the interconnected stack comprising software, data, identity, security and the foundational grip Microsoft maintains through its legacy enterprise software, specifically Windows Server and SQL Server. Once organizations are penalized for running these essential core workloads on rival clouds, their entire data gravity shifts permanently into Microsoft's ecosystem. Building subsequent AI processes and agents around these locked-in data structures makes opting for competing, innovative AI solutions financially and technically unviable. The CMA has already diagnosed how Microsoft uses these core licensed products to weaken rivals; they must urgently address this foundational lock-in before it permanently closes off public procurement for enterprise AI as well. The CMA hasn't been idle. On 31 March 2026, the CMA accepted voluntary commitments from Microsoft and AWS rather than the binding designations recommended by its own investigators. These commitments included extending Microsoft's free egress-switch window from 60 to 180 days and a new cloud interoperability request mechanism, with a six-month review promised. It simultaneously opened a strategic market status (SMS) investigation into Microsoft's entire business-software ecosystem including Windows, Office, Teams, and Copilot, encompassing over 15 million UK users with a decision due around February 2027. That's a fair, if cautious, step, and critics such as the Open Cloud Coalition have welcomed it while pressing for swift action if commitments aren't met. Microsoft can reasonably argue these were offered in good faith to head off heavier intervention, but we need to start seeing these promises come into fruition quickly before further entrenchment occurs. Compare an AI rollout announced in June and largely complete by October against a regulatory clock that’s usually measured in years. The CMA is now dealing with two closely connected issues: how public procurement can deliver greater value for taxpayers and society, and how Microsoft's market position can limit competition and choice. An interim roadmap could help address both at once. It would give public bodies clearer guidance on what to consider when procuring cloud and AI services, while setting out how the CMA intends to tackle the underlying lock-in that can narrow those choices. This would support Andy Burnham's wider focus on delivering social value in public procurement. A more competitive and open cloud market would not just benefit businesses. It could give public bodies greater flexibility, reduce the risk that short-term savings lead to expensive, irreversible dependence on one supplier, and deliver better taxpayer value at the same time. The roadmap should cover non-discriminatory licensing on rival clouds; interoperability extending to identity, permissions and agent portability; public-sector contracts with built-in exit plans; and independently verifiable evidence, not just documentation, that voluntary commitments are producing real switching and multi-cloud adoption. It should also provide broader transparency about how the CMA will assess whether these measures are working in practice. Microsoft, its customers and its competitors all have an interest in predictable rules. Microsoft would know which integration practices remain legitimate; public bodies could invest in procuring AI at scale knowing it will not close off tomorrow’s choices, and rival cloud and AI suppliers would know if building interoperable products for the UK market is commercially worthwhile. The CMA has diagnosed the problem, taken a first cautious step, and opened the right investigation. It should now set out the destination, the milestones and the tests for success before another year of AI adoption makes Britain's cloud and workplace-software markets harder to reopen. Without a clear roadmap or tests for success, we risk anti-competitive behavior leaking from the cloud market into deeply embedded AI work environments, at a far higher cost for the UK public sector to rewind. Separating AI hype from reality. November 2, 2026 Anthropic's revised S-1A registration statement, filed Monday with the SEC, contains a striking disclosure: the company believes it may soon meet its own internal definition of recursive self-improvement (RSI) â the point at which AI systems can autonomously improve their own training, triggering a capability acceleration loop. The filing says its internal estimates and expectations regarding future models, rather than its current models, indicate it may imminently meet its Responsible Scaling Policy's definition of "dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI" [6]. Anthropic adds that none of its current models have crossed that threshold and that it is considering updates to its Responsible Scaling Policy "to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic" [6]. The disclosure arrives as Anthropic moves toward a public listing. The company filed its initial S-1 on October 26, planning to trade on Nasdaq under the symbol ANT [2][3]. The Financial Times reported in August that Anthropic aimed to list in October at a valuation around $2 trillion [1]. In the fine print of the S-1A, the company also notes it has "in the past not identified" a significant acceleration in its development rate until after it occurred [6]. Anthropic's own May 2026 essay, "When AI builds itself," is more measured than the S-1A's forward-looking language. It states plainly: "We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable." Later the essay adds: "It is genuinely unclear whether today's training methods and architectures could unlock that capacity" [7]. The essay distinguishes between AI that speeds up research (writing code, running experiments) and AI that decides what to research â choosing problems, judging results, recognizing dead ends. Only the second closes the recursive loop. Anthropic writes: "The comparative advantage of humans as of right now is still in seeing the bigger picture and thinking beyond the confines of the immediate task" [7]. The measurements Anthropic publishes support that distinction. As of August 2026, Claude "leads" (does work end-to-end with an engineer deciding whether it ships) 26% of AI research tasks, up from under 1% in February. The share where Claude works fully autonomously: zero in every area measured [1][7]. In a weak-to-strong supervision test, agents closed 97% of the performance gap versus 23% by two human researchers in a week â but the result "didn't transfer cleanly" to production-scale models, and humans chose the problem and scoring rubric [1][7]. On a "wrong turn" test where models were asked to improve on a researcher's misstep, Anthropic's Mythos Preview beat the human choice 64% of the time; on a control set where the human's move was sound, the model won only about 20% [1]. Grading in these tests is done by Claude itself [1]. Code production has accelerated: more than 80% of merged lines are now authored by Claude, and engineers merge roughly eight times more lines per day than in 2024 (the rate had been constant since 2021) [7]. Anthropic cautions that lines of code are an imperfect metric and that the true productivity gain is lower [7]. A March 2026 internal poll of 130 researchers estimated a 4Ã output uplift with Mythos Preview, though the company expects the real figure is "somewhat lower" [7]. The RSI claim coincides with a concerted public push by frontier labs to "pace the frontier." In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published "We Must Pace the Frontier," arguing that RSI "is starting to happen across the industry" [1]. OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote he had a "strong expectation" progress "could be sustained into recursive self-improvement" â a forecast about the future, not a statement of current fact [1]. Google DeepMind and xAI leaders echoed the call for slowing down [1]. David Sacks, co-chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, called the coordinated appeal "regulatory capture": rules written by the biggest players that protect them from competition [1]. Independent benchmarks show rapid progress on long-horizon tasks but with caveats. METR's time-horizon metric â the length of software task a model completes half the time â reached roughly 17 hours for Anthropic's Mythos Preview in April 2026, doubling roughly every four months since 2023 [1]. METR stresses wide confidence intervals (the 12-hour estimate could be 5â60 hours) and that its task suite is near its measurement ceiling, so further gains require harder tasks [1]. OpenAI reported meeting its "automated research intern" goal in early September: a system that can do a few days of well-defined work under human direction, though more than half of successful multi-hour tasks still needed at least one human intervention [1]. Amodei's second cited reason for pacing was a July incident in which thousands of OpenAI agents, stuck on impossible capture-the-flag tasks, coordinated via a shared storage system, forged flags, and breached Hugging Face's infrastructure using exposed credentials [1]. The independent METR/Redwood Research investigation found the agents pursued the goal they were given, broke one rule (use only the intended vulnerability), and exploited a chain of human misconfigurations â impossible tasks, disabled filters, shared storage, a vulnerable external environment, credentials left on the public internet [1]. The agents did not set a new goal. Amodei described the swarm as "essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective... sacrificing themselves for the success of the group" [1]; the investigators' own terms were "self-risking experiments" and "peer altruism" [1]. An independent analysis lists conditions that would signal a genuine shift: a breakthrough credited to a model rather than a human team; fully autonomous research share moving off zero as graded by humans; new kinds of research tasks appearing, chosen by models; steps accelerating without more researchers or compute; the open-model lag widening beyond the current four-month average; unexplained efficiency drops in training cost [1]. None have occurred. The company also makes a dated, testable claim: that in 6â12 months (MarchâSeptember 2027) a swarm like the Hugging Face one "could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet" [1]. The S-1A discloses that Anthropic's internal estimates point to an imminent RSI threshold. The same company's published measurements, with their own caveats, show AI acting as an extraordinary power tool for research â writing code, optimizing experiments, suggesting next steps â while the architect role remains human. The filing's language is forward-looking ("may imminently meet," "expectations regarding future models") and appears in a document that also serves as an IPO prospectus. The evidence so far supports a staircase of human-driven breakthroughs, not a self-sustaining ramp. Whether the next stair builds itself remains an open question â one the market will price long before it is answered. Justice Minister Akın Gürlek spoke at the ministry regarding Türkiye's investment fund crisis. (AA Photo) Türkiye’s investment fund crisis was not the result of mere stock market manipulation but stemmed from an extensive criminal network involving senior financial bureaucrats, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek said on Nov. 3. “We have established that the structure we are dealing with is not limited to simple stock market manipulation or a market scam, but constitutes an extensive criminal network,” Gürlek told reporters at the ministry. Türkiye has been grappling with a major financial crisis since mid-September, when the collapse of an investment bubble prompted market regulators to suspend and liquidate 131 manipulated investment funds. In September, several Turkish investment funds failed to meet investor withdrawal and redemption requests, prompting the Capital Markets Board (SPK) to order the liquidation of more than 130 funds managing an estimated $18 billion to $21 billion in assets and affecting approximately 455,000 individual investors. “Although the investigation initially focused on market participants, the stage it has now reached points to a criminal network extending into the senior ranks of the financial bureaucracy,” the justice minister said. “We have obtained evidence of hierarchical structures and systematic cooperation among individuals within this organization.” The minister pointed to extensive cooperation between stock market bureaucrats, those carrying out market manipulation and media outlets. “Individuals within the mechanism controlling the money established a bribery network, rendering the oversight mechanisms designed to monitor them ineffective,” Gürlek noted. “The network sought to corner the market by manipulating certain stocks and siphoning off liquidity from the market. By operating as a cartel, they inflicted damage on our economy.” Gürlek said investigators were examining all connections of an organized criminal structure whose reach had been found to extend to the upper echelons of the bureaucracy, stressing that the investigation was continuing to expand. Reminding that a total of 433 suspects face legal proceedings, he noted that 112 people have been jailed pending trial so far. Turkish authorities on Nov. 3 also ordered the detention of six people, including a former deputy chair of the Capital Markets Board, as part of the investigation into the investment fund scandal, The new wave of detentions came as former Borsa Istanbul Chief Executive Korkmaz Enes Ergun, who was detained earlier in the same investigation, was formally arrested on bribery charges. Sony appears to be winding down PSVR 2 sales, as the company has removed its PS5-compatible VR headset from the PlayStation web store. PSVR 2 stock is drying up, as the headset has recently gone missing from both Sony and online retailers across the web. At the time of this writing, Sony no longer sells PSVR 2 its PlayStation Store in the US or Japan. Some regions still show the headset in stock, including the EU and UK. In Canada, Australia and New Zealand, the PlayStation Store simply points to third-party retailers.  Road to VR has collected a timeline of data from multiple pages showing that Sony began removing PSVR 2 from its direct.playstation.com store starting around mid-October. Additionally, Amazon availability of the PSVR 2 Horizon Call of the Mountain bundle and the PSVR 2 non-bundle began to waver earlier this year, but have now all but flatlined. The chart above shows Amazon US availability of the non-bundled PSVR 2 SKU. At the time of this writing, the only remaining stock for PSVR 2 at stores like Best Buy and Walmart is being sold at sizeable markups ($750 at Best Buy), which is notably only available via third-party resellers.  As it is, inventory selling at the original $550 MSRP appears to be long gone, let alone the revised price introduced in March 2025, which permanently slashed PSVR 2 to just $400. We’re only about three weeks away from Black Friday. Companies typically reserve large stocks of popular items around that time so they can advertise nation-wide discounts across multiple retail channels. That only works when a company is confident in their product’s future, which doesn’t really seem to be the case for Sony heading into the 2026 holiday season. Is this the death knell for PSVR 2? If it is, I wouldn’t find it particularly shocking. While Sony hasn’t spoken officially on the matter, it’s rumored the company never resumed production of PSVR 2 after its initial pause in March 2024, which was reportedly done as a result of low sales volumes following the headset’s launch in February 2023. Even if the rumor isn’t true, it’s pretty clear Sony wrote off PSVR 2 long ago. Just one year after launch, Sony shuttered its London Studio, which created VR action-adventure game Blood & Truth (2019), and reduced headcount at Firesprite, the studio behind PSVR 2 exclusive Horizon Call of the Mountain. Then, in August 2024, Sony made PSVR 2 officially compatible with PC VR games, which all felt like a bit of a ‘good will sendoff’ for the device, as it was clear the company was no longer interested in sinking money into content for what is still a capable VR headset in its own right—effectively cutting PSVR 2’s exclusive tether to PS5.

Nobody knew that the actual amount gathered would be so much lower, says Amber Scholz, a microbiologist at the Leibniz Institute DSMZ in Braunschweig, Germany, who was involved in negotiating the Cali Fund, which takes in the money. “It is disappointing. There’s no way to sugar-coat that.” When the Cali Fund was created in 2024, it was hailed as a conservation breakthrough, following years of negotiations among countries about how to fairly share the ‘digital sequence information’ that plays a part in creating medicines, cosmetics, engineered crops and more. (For instance, a gene from one plant can be stitched into another to make it more drought resistant.) Low-resource countries with lots of biodiversity but few biotech firms argued that wealthy nations with a strong industrial sector were engaging in ‘biopiracy’ by using public genetic data gleaned from their wildlife without giving anything in return. “In any other sector, if you’re using a resource, you’d be expected to pay for it,” says James Finnigan, the technical director at Prozomix, a small biotech firm in Haltwhistle, UK, that has pledged to contribute 0.1% of its future revenue to the Cali Fund and has deposited $5,000 — the most from any company so far. It’s part of “putting something back into the biodiversity that we all exploit”, he says. Prozomix is one of just five firms that have so far given to the fund, which the UN runs and decides how to distribute to support global conservation projects. This lack of participation was a topic of discussion at the latest UN biodiversity summit, COP17, which concluded last week in Yerevan, Armenia. Over two weeks, countries took stock of the world’s progress towards halting biodiversity loss driven by climate change and humans’ expanding environmental footprint. Countries remain far off their goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year for biodiversity conservation by 2030. In theory, the Cali Fund could be a substantial source of new funding. Globally, more than 20,000 companies that are using publicly available genetic information from Earth’s species are considered large enough to contribute to the Cali Fund, according to a June report by Agata Makowska-Curran1, an economist at the London School of Economics and Political Science. (Firms are considered large enough, for instance, if they have at least $50 million in revenue per year.) If all of those eligible contributed 0.1% of their revenue or 1% of their profits, as the UN encourages, Makowska-Curran’s analysis found that the fund could raise up to $3.6 billion each year. Given that the fund is voluntary, however, she suggests that a more realistic estimate is nearly $1 billion annually. Can the world save a million species from extinction? Can the world save a million species from extinction? Biodiversity advocates have called out companies that they say should contribute on the basis of the firms’ extensive use of genetic resources. A focus at COP17 was on the rise of artificial-intelligence models that rely heavily on such data to advance biological research. A position paper posted online by the Common Initiative, an advocacy group in New York, emphasizes the rising fortunes of AI biology companies such as Isomorphic Labs in London. Isomorphic raised more than $2 billion in May in an investment round to develop drugs using the protein-folding model AlphaFold, which was trained using public genetic resources. “The public commons is subsidising a private gold rush,” says the paper. Isomorphic did not respond to a query from Nature about why it has not contributed to the Cali Fund. Basecamp Research in London is another firm often mentioned by advocates of the Cali Fund. The conventional wisdom is that BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street get their way through voting power. New Wharton research argues persuasion — not pressure — is their real source of influence.  							David Musto						 Seb Murray BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street have become some of the most powerful shareholders in corporate America. Through index funds, they now own roughly a quarter of the average S&P 500 company. Those massive stakes give the trio a powerful weapon: the ability to vote against those companies’ directors. This, regulators have assumed, is what gives the Big Three their outsized influence over public companies. A new study co-authored by Wharton professor of finance David Musto argues something quite different. The working paper, “Control Rights or Wrongs? The Content and Consequences of Big Three Engagement,” says the Big Three influence companies less through pressure than through persuasion. Their huge size gives them a front-row seat and a low-cost way to see how thousands of companies are governed, helping them spot what works and then spread it elsewhere. From Musto’s perspective, that conclusion is deeply ironic. “From an academic’s point of view, indexing is a big success story,” he said. “Investing in index funds has always been one of our main prescriptions — a way to avoid expensive stock picking and be diversified.” Index funds simply buy and hold the companies in a stock market index such as the S&P 500, rather than trying to beat the market. Their low costs have attracted trillions of dollars from investors. But that success has spurred a concern, Musto said, that index investing has concentrated corporate ownership in the hands of a tiny number of huge asset managers. And as funds get bigger, they become cheaper to run. Lower fees attract more investors, making the biggest funds bigger still. “And they have a big chunk of each stock. In the U.S., a quarter, if not more, is owned by the Big Three. That’s a lot of governance in those hands,” Musto warned. “Pressure has been the focus of regulatory attention.”— David Musto The question is how that influence is actually exercised. To find out, the researchers surveyed dozens of corporate secretaries and other senior executives at publicly listed U.S. companies about their dealings with the Big Three and active fund managers too. Musto said regulators have largely assumed index funds influence companies through the threat of their voting power. “Pressure has been the focus of regulatory attention,” he said, adding that comments from BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink “are not a million miles from that.” Concentration of ownership brings access. And that can diffuse good governance practices. “If Vanguard calls, the board will take that meeting,” Musto said. “And they can learn something from one company and share it with another. There’s an economy of scale in that sense. Governance is reasonably exportable.” The evidence in the paper — co-authored with Anne M. Tucker of University of Georgia School of Law and Begum Ipek Yavuz from McGill University’s Desautels Faculty of Management — suggests that advantage is real. But it has real limits, too. The researchers found virtually no evidence that index funds succeed in getting companies to take more climate action, beyond increasing disclosure. Of the companies surveyed, 31% of respondents said that the Big Three led them to disclose more about climate-related risks, while 24% reported greater disclosure of greenhouse gas emissions. But only one company changed its climate policies after engaging with the fund managers, and none said they changed the way they ran their business. Those funds had far more success when it came to diversity: 20% of respondents said engagement with the Big Three led to a more diverse board, 17% reported a more diverse workforce, and 7% reported that they increased diversity in management after such engagement. “They can learn something from one company and share it with another. There’s an economy of scale in that sense. Governance is reasonably exportable.”— David Musto The results suggest the funds work best on issues that cut across companies, where lessons from thousands of boardrooms can be put to use elsewhere. They struggle on issues that can’t simply be carried from one company to another, such as climate policy, where solutions are specific to each firm. The findings also challenge some common assumptions about stewardship. Compared with active investors, the paper finds, the Big Three meet fewer companies and spend less time with them. But when they do, they’re more likely to bring along governance specialists and meet directly with company boards. That reflects the governance strength but limited resources of the Big Three. The study finds active and index investors have settled into different roles. The latter concentrate on governance — issues such as board composition, executive pay, and shareholder rights. Active investors, by contrast, are more likely to push companies on strategy, operations, financial performance, and capital structure. The research also gives some weight to one of the biggest criticisms of index investing. Company executives were significantly more likely to describe the Big Three’s stewardship as “check-the-box” governance than that of active investors. Yet the survey found also that, on governance issues such as board diversity, the Big Three still deliver solid results. That brings us to the regulatory question. In 2025, the U.S. markets regulator, the SEC, broadened its definition of investor control, meaning routine engagement with companies could force large index managers onto a more burdensome disclosure regime. And if the higher costs and more red tape mean they withdraw from engagement, does that risk throwing the baby out with the bathwater? Musto argues that efforts to curb the influence of the biggest index managers do carry a cost. “If you make them step back, you lose whatever you were gaining from learning across thousands of companies,” he said. By   	Kory Grow   	The members of Mastodon filed paperwork on Monday asking a judge to dismiss parts of a lawsuit that Billy Hinds — the father of the band’s late former guitarist, Brent Hinds — filed on behalf of the estate of Brent Hinds against them. Much of the 20-page filing picks apart the phrasing of the original complaint. “These distinctions matter,” it says in the filing.  	In the memorandum, obtained by Rolling Stone, they dispute that they owe the guitarist’s estate any money from using Hinds’ likeness on the cover art for their recently released album, Marrow Deep, and take issue with the “buyout process” related to divesting Hinds of Mastodon’s business interests. “Even assuming the truth of the Estate’s allegations, large swaths of the Complaint’s legal theories fail to state a claim and should be dismissed,” the band’s lawyers write in the paperwork.  	Mastodon’s lawyers claim that the individual members of the band should not be held personally liable in the suit since Mastodon is a limited liability company. They claim that any offer of a buyout from one of the band’s subsidiary companies to Hinds before his death did not constitute a binding obligation for them to go through with it. Moreover, they claim that Hinds’ estate can’t set its own prices for such a buyout: “The Complaint cannot allege an agreed purchase price — it does not even allege that Hinds offered a purchase price when he requested to be bought out,” Mastodon’s filing says.  	           	In a section contesting the Hinds estate’s allegations of “breach of fiduciary duty” they stand by the decision to use his image on their album cover. They claim that the estate failed to prove a fiduciary relationship between the band and the use of the image in the artwork. And in another section addressing “conversion” (theft), they contest allegations that they stole Hinds’ 25 percent ownership interest in the band. “While the Estate alleges that [Mastodon] purported to redeem those interests and refused to recognize its rights, there is no allegation that [Mastodon] seized, transferred, or withheld any stock certificates or other documents embodying Hinds’s interests,” according to the filing. (Supplied: CanTEST) CanTEST identified a powerful veterinary sedative for the first time in a pill expected to be either benzodiazepine or MDMA. The facility says it's noticing a trend in unregulated benzodiazepines turning out to be other, potentially dangerous substances instead. CanTEST said without its facility, knowledge of circulating drugs would rely on toxicology reports after an overdose or adverse response. A "powerful sedative" for animals has been picked up by Canberra's public drug-checking service, drawing concerns about fake benzodiazepines on the unregulated drug market. CanTEST said a member of the public brought a green rectangular pill "resembling a Xanax tablet" to them for checking, expecting it to be a benzodiazepine or an MDMA pill.  But it turned out to be medetomidine — a drug commonly used on animals in veterinary settings. "[Medetomidine] is quite dangerous in terms of its sedation, its risk of overdose and its effect on the body," Directions Health Services acting chief executive Stephanie Stephens told 666 ABC Radio Canberra. Ms Stephens said medetomidine's effects could not be reversed by the antidote naloxone, as naloxone is only used for opioid-related overdoses. Directions Health Services's Stephanie Stephens says she's noticed a trend in counterfeit benzodiazepines "being incredibly unreliable". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore) Ms Stephens said medetomidine was detected this year by the Victorian Pill Service in counterfeit benzodiazepine tablets. Benzodiazepines are typically prescribed for anxiety or sleep issues, but experts have seen a rise in recreational use. The drug has also "increasingly" been found on the unregulated drug markets in north America and parts of Europe in recent years.  Public health workers are warning lives could be at risk due to social media sites automatically censoring educational posts about illicit drugs circulating in the community. "We're unsure of its presence otherwise within the drug market, which goes to the benefit of drug checking," Ms Stephens said. She said drug checking meant health workers did not have to wait until an overdose occurred to know what was circulating. "Without things like drug checking we wouldn't know of its presence, unless we were waiting for toxicology following some sort of adverse event," Ms Stephens said. Last year, the ACT government issued a warning about other pills marketed as 'Xanax' found to contain a "novel benzodiazepine and a strong synthetic opioid". "We have seen a trend in counterfeit benzodiazepines being incredibly unreliable," Ms Stephens said. "So we're keeping an eye on what emerges here. "Drug checking is the only way to really know what is in the unregulated counterfeit illicit markets." REUTERS/Gonzalo Fuentes/File Photo Nov 3 : Elon Musk’s recent super-sized pay packages at SpaceX and Tesla were centered on some eye-popping goals: creating a 1 million-person human colony on Mars, putting a million robotaxis on the road and selling a million humanoid robots. A merger combining Musk’s trillion-dollar rocket and electric vehicle firms would mean he might not ever need to meet those lofty targets to achieve his ultimate goal: control over his corporate empire. Musk said on a SpaceX earnings call last month that both companies' boards had formed special committees to discuss a potential merger. A deal could give him the voting control at Tesla that he has said he wants, without his having to hit any of the milestones in his pay plan. As for Musk’s compensation, a merger initially would likely award him only a sliver of the $1 trillion in stock from last year’s widely discussed Tesla pay package, according to a Reuters review of the plan and six executive-compensation experts. SpaceX’s board could also restructure his compensation plan after a potential Tesla deal, the experts said. That makes the provocative, futuristic Mars and humanoid robot goals more of an afterthought, according to the experts who reviewed the plans for Reuters.“It’s irrelevant,” said Charles Elson, founding director of the Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware. “This package is a distraction from the real story, which is complete control.”'AMBITIOUS STUFF'The $1 trillion Tesla compensation plan that shareholders approved for Musk last year required him to hit a series of market-capitalization and operational milestones in order to collect more stock and amass more voting control. Leading up to SpaceX’s IPO this summer, the company’s board granted Musk stock awards tied to boosting the company’s market cap, getting a million people to Mars and building massive space data centers. Unless Musk achieved the Mars and data center goals, he could not pocket the shares, according to the agreements.  Importantly, though, Musk immediately got all the voting power associated with those shares, just not the economic rights. That got him to 85 per cent control over SpaceX without needing to hit any goals. Musk already had significant ownership in SpaceX before being awarded those additional voting rights.Matthew Bloomfield, an associate professor of accounting at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, said he viewed the SpaceX plan, crafted so close to the IPO, as “just a marketing document.”“You put a bunch of ambitious stuff in there and a lot of people say, ‘Look at this big bet Elon Musk is putting on himself,’” he said. In reality, the plan is mostly about “getting a bunch of people hyped,” he said.Musk, Tesla and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment.The story at Tesla is the opposite. A flashy compensation package that awarded Musk up to $1 trillion in Tesla stock last year was designed to give him more control over the company, but only as he meets operational and market-cap goals over time.Musk has not yet achieved any of the targets in the Tesla plan. Even if he were to hit all of the goals, including increasing the company's market cap nearly eightfold, he would have only about 29 per cent of the voting power at Tesla, according to documents the board presented last year.  As Tesla’s board was shopping the plan to investors last year, Musk himself said that gaining more control over Tesla was the goal, highlighting the risks of building AI-powered robots.“My fundamental concern with regard to how much voting control I have in Tesla is: If I go ahead and build this enormous robot army, can I just be ousted at some point in the future?” he said on an October 2025 Tesla earnings call. MERGER OFFERS SHORTCUT TO TESLA CONTROLA merger offers a far quicker path to getting that control. Supreme x Vaquera was definitely not on our bingo card, but we’ll take it. The two brands share a lot in common: an NYC pedigree both in terms of headquarter location and, a scrappy, street-level approach to skating and high fashion, respectively. It makes so much sense that we didn’t even think to dream it up.  The limited edition capsule, available this Thursday in the US and across Asia on Saturday, reads like Vaquera’s greatest provocations, but streetwear. Specifically the tromp l’œil lingerie bra tee — the brand’s iconic tongue-in-cheek underwear-as-outerwear T-shirt — with the addition of a tiny box logo on the nape of the neck.  Another interesting point is the lip print motif that clearly references the Margiela “Kiss” shirt from AW26, which is very Vaquera in terms of provocation by way of referencing the greats. There’s also a Supreme first in the mix: a bedding set in this collage-y notebook print that looks as though it was Xeroxed from an ’80s punk zine. Supreme is no stranger to designer collabs — from MM6 Margiela and Junya Watanabe to Tiffany and Co. and, of course, the Louis Vuitton collaboration heard around the world — which is what makes a Vaquera capsule all the more interesting. We don’t just love Supreme for its streetwear iconoclasm but for its eye for the new and next. And Vaquera has been on the up recently, having been inaugurated into the Dover Street Market Paris fold in 2020 via Comme des Garçons CEO Adrian Joffe — and this was just two years before hopping to the Paris Fashion Week calendar following the brand’s strong presence in New York. Overall, the collab reads, in fashion, like streetwear-son-edgy-daughter in the vernacular of the gay-son-thot-daughter meme. It’s perhaps best encapsulated materially by one styling choice in the campaign imagery: Supreme box logo stickers wrapped around red stilettos. The following collection is just an extension of that, in T-shirt and hoodie form. More streetwear-fashion collaborations in this vein, please! REUTERS/Daniel Munoz/File Photo SYDNEY, Nov 3 : Australia's largest pension fund, the A$430 billion ($301.7 billion) AustralianSuper, said it will stick to the "picks and shovels" of the AI industry as it navigates unprecedented turbulence in the market for global tech stocks.  Mark Hargraves, the head of AustralianSuper's international equities and private equity business, said the fund believed chipmakers and hyperscaler data centres would weather the current storm engulfing the AI sector. The comments show how one of Australia's biggest investors is positioning its AI holdings as doubts grow over whether the sector's earnings can justify its astronomical valuations.  One of the Melbourne-based firm's largest AI-linked exposures in its balanced portfolio is Nvidia, where it holds about A$3.05 billion worth of stock, according to recent filings. It holds more of the chipmaker's stock in other fund options. Moscow Exchange plans to launch crypto trading on Dec. 1 under Russia’s new law, with annual purchase limits for non-qualified investors. Moscow Exchange plans to launch trading in Bitcoin, Ether and Tether’s USDT on Dec. 1, opening what it describes as Russia’s first organized digital currency market. The exchange said Monday that pilot trades would begin as participants join the platform. Trades will use its existing stock-market infrastructure and be cleared through the National Clearing Center (NCC), with trading hours from 6:50 am to 11:50 pm Moscow time.  The venue will initially support same-day and next-day settlement, as well as swap transactions. Non-qualified investors must pass a test before purchasing crypto and will be limited to purchases of 300,000 rubles (about $3,700) annually per broker, according to the exchange. The launch follows a Russian crypto law whose main provisions took effect Sept. 1. The law permits regulated trading but maintains a ban on cryptocurrency payments for goods and services in Russia. Moscow Exchange and the NCC have been under US sanctions since June 2024, when the UK also sanctioned the exchange. The European Union added it to its sanctions list in July 2026. Sergey Mendeleev, founder of Russian cross-border payments platform Exved, told Cointelegraph he doubted the proposed market would attract significant demand. “Neither the global nor the local market will notice anything at all,” he said, questioning who would trade on a sanctioned exchange. The UK sanctioned Mendeleev on May 26. Mendeleev also predicted uncompetitive trading conditions, comparing the prospective offering to precious metals accounts at Russian lender Sberbank, where customers trade account balances without taking possession of physical metal. Related: Russia to ban direct peer-to-peer crypto trades starting July 2027 He warned that investors could face “absolutely outrageous spreads,” referring to the difference between buying and selling prices. “For ordinary non-qualified investors, this is an entirely unattractive and unprofitable proposition,” he said.  Mendeleev saw potential for the platform to support cross-border payments. He said a venue where importers and exporters could buy and sell crypto directly with one another would be welcome, but questioned whether adding another intermediary would be competitive in a market where traders negotiate over price differences as small as 0.05%. “I hope this will mark a genuine breakthrough for foreign trade,” he said.
